sections.text:
The central construction is more specific than a thermal product identity. With the specified clock and positive surface gravity, the paper adopts
\[
L=\frac{c^2}{\kappa},\qquad U(A,L)=\frac{Ac^2\kappa}{8\pi G}=\frac{c^4A}{8\pi GL}.
\]
For independent area and length, the checked derivatives give
\[
\Pi=\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial A}\right)_L=\frac{c^4}{8\pi GL},\qquad F_L=-\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial L}\right)_A=\frac{Ac^4}{8\pi GL^2}=\frac UL=M_U\kappa.
\]
Thus
\[
dU=\Pi\,dA-F_L\,dL,\qquad P_L=\frac{F_L}{A}=\frac{\Pi}{L}=\frac{\kappa^2}{8\pi G}.
\]
Here \(\Pi\) is a surface-stress coefficient with energy-per-area units, whereas \(P_L\) has ordinary pressure units. The selected normal-scale response is \(-\int d\tau\,dA\,P_L\delta L\); for a common uniform source variation its area integral is the force. This is a generalized boundary response, not a claim of a new material interaction.

The source correctly retains both legs of the complete differential and distinguishes its negative length contribution from the positive-work convention. It also checks \(A\,d\Pi=-F_LdL\). Neither \(AL\) nor the equal products \(\Pi A\), \(F_LL\), and \(P_LAL\) automatically constitute independent volumes or energy stores.

sections.text:
The supplied geometric checks derive the coordinate map
\[
(X^0,X^1)=(\rho+c^2/a)\bigl(\sinh(a\tau/c),\cosh(a\tau/c)\bigr)
\]
and the metric
\[
ds^2=-c^2(1+a\rho/c^2)^2d\tau^2+d\rho^2+dy^2+dz^2.
\]
The reference observer at \(\rho=0\) has proper time \(\tau\) and proper acceleration \(a\). Constant-\(\tau\) slices are orthogonal to that observer. Integrating their normal line element to the wedge boundary gives \(c^2/a\), while transverse patch area is independent of the normal scale. These actual computations substantiate line 38 and the normalization used in lines 29–30.

The result privileges this length geometrically for this observer and simultaneity convention. It does not establish the same proper-distance interpretation for Schwarzschild or arbitrary curved horizons. Other scalar coordinates remain permissible when their response coefficients transform accordingly.

sections.text:
The one-page source explicitly imposes a fixed clock, fixed cuts, a selected mixed prescription, and both \(\theta=0\) and \(\delta\theta=0\). Its cited companion, Horizon Boundary Mechanics: Force, Pressure, and Work from the Einstein Boundary Potential, Section 3, pages 2–3, Equations (10)–(17), supplies an explicit scalar source \(\mu=\widehat\kappa+\theta/2\), area polarization, exact boundary exchange, and physical-clock dictionary.

The supplied trusted kernel independently computes the local EH boundary flux from all 64 connection variations in a fixed Gaussian-null chart. With the stated orientation and in geometric units, it obtains the scalar/shear/exact decomposition underlying
\[
\Theta_{\rm EH}=\frac1{8\pi G}\int\left[-\mu\,\delta\epsilon_S+\frac{\epsilon_S}{2}\sigma^{AB}\delta q_{AB}+\delta\{\epsilon_S(\widehat\kappa+\theta)\}\right]du.
\]
For the specified functionals \(B_0=\int\epsilon_S(\widehat\kappa+\theta)du/(8\pi G)\) and \(B_\mu=\int\epsilon_S\mu\,du/(8\pi G)\), the action choice \(I_{\rm rate}=I_{\rm EH}-B_0+B_\mu\) gives the scalar rate form \(\int\epsilon_S\delta\mu\,du/(8\pi G)\), with shear response retained separately. This implements, rather than merely names, the polarization change.

The endpoint identity is also checked: \(B_\mu-B_0=-(A_f-A_i)/(16\pi G)\). Tangent nonexpansion throughout the fixed interval implies \(\delta A_f=\delta A_i\), not that each area must be fixed. Other global corner and matter responses remain controlled premises, not terms declared universally absent.

Restoring \(du=c\,d\tau\), \(\widehat\kappa=\kappa/c^2\), and the EH action normalization gives \(Ac^2\delta\kappa/(8\pi G)\) per unit physical time for the common stationary scalar mode. The checked pullback then yields
\[
\frac{\Theta_\kappa^{(0)}}{\Delta\tau}=\frac{Ac^2}{8\pi G}\delta\kappa=-\frac{Ac^4}{8\pi GL^2}\delta L=-F_L\delta L.
\]
The reduced fixed-interval generating-functional derivative is checked as \(-\Delta\tau F_L\). The companion's Section 3.1, Equations (18)–(21), supplies the consistently oriented stationary area–boost representation; its coefficient is checked as well.

The primary passages are compatible with this restricted route: Hopfmüller–Freidel displays the scalar conjugacy and exact variations, and Odak et al., Equation (3.34), shows why different polarizations must not be conflated. Parattu et al., Equations (111)–(113), supplies an earlier static response with the same coefficient, also supported by the separate supplied static-metric calculation. The kernel's negative controls correctly show that nonexpansion alone does not suppress shear, the selected one-form is not all of \(\delta U\), and the same U does not uniquely select an action. None contradicts the manuscript's selected-sector formulation.

sections.text:
For the stated infinity-normalized Schwarzschild family, \(A=4\pi R^2\), \(L=2R\), and \(U=Mc^2/2\). Taking the independent-coordinate response before restricting gives \(F_L=c^4/(8G)\). Transforming the work afterward gives
\[
F_R=2F_L=M\kappa,\qquad P_R=\frac{F_R}{4\pi R^2}=2P_L=\frac{\kappa^2}{4\pi G}.
\]
All factors are checked. Since \(dL/L=dR/R\), this is the same fractional horizon-size change, not displacement of another surface at \(2R\).

The thermal inputs give \(TS=U\), while \(F_LL=U\), so \(Mc^2=TS+F_LL\) is correct. The companion, Section 5.2, explicitly treats this as coincident products associated with different directions of one potential, not separately stored energies. Along the constrained family, the area contribution is twice the positive length work; consequently \(dU=F_LdL\) and \(d(Mc^2)=T\,dS=2F_LdL\). This is consistent with the negative fixed-area length derivative because area changes simultaneously. Adding the length term independently to the mass first law would double-count a variation, but the manuscript does not do so.
sections.title: Schwarzschild work conversion and the unchanged mass first law

sections.text:
The cosmological sector adopts instantaneous equilibrium, \(L=R_A\), positive temperature \(T_{\rm CK}=\hbar c/(2\pi k_BR_A)\), spherical area and areal volume, and Einstein–Misner–Sharp energy \(E=c^4R_A/(2G)=\rho V\). These are accepted sector inputs. The checked consequences are
\[
P_{\rm screen}=P_L=\frac{c^4}{8\pi GR_A^2}=\frac\rho3,\qquad dE=T_{\rm CK}dS-P_{\rm screen}dV.
\]
The radius coefficients make the identity transparent: \(dE/dR_A=c^4/(2G)\), \(T_{\rm CK}dS/dR_A=c^4/G\), and \(P_{\rm screen}dV/dR_A=c^4/(2G)\).

Cai–Kim, Section 2 around its dynamical-temperature discussion, uses the inverse-radius equilibrium calibration and explicitly qualifies its interpretation for an evolving horizon. Akbar–Cai instead develops the moving-horizon unified identity \(dE=T_{\rm dyn}dS+W dV\), with \(W=(\rho-p_m)/2\) and a dynamical surface gravity containing \(1-\dot R_A/(2HR_A)\). Its signed temperature/orientation convention must accompany that identity. Neither \(W\) nor that dynamical temperature is automatically the manuscript's positive CK screen assignment. Akbar–Cai's conclusion also distinguishes total enclosed-energy change from Cai–Kim's matter-supply heat-flux notation.

The submitted page does not equate these incompatible coefficients or processes. Lines 79–80 expressly exclude a stationary-worldtube interpretation for evolving FRW. Consequently the stationary canonical restriction must not be imposed on this separately declared screen-state assignment.

Finally, substituting \(\rho=3P\) into the established Einstein equations gives the printed expansion, acceleration, and conservation forms, including \(H^2+kc^2/a^2=(8\pi G/c^2)P\). Their scalar rewrites are checked. Bulk pressure remains \(p_m\), as line 66 states; \(P=\rho/3\) is not a bulk equation of state. Exact screen-state algebra does not establish exact equilibrium thermality for arbitrary cosmological evolution, but the manuscript's stated assignment does not require that stronger claim.
sections.title: FRW screen pressure is coherent under the separate CK assignment

sections.text:
The closest prior result is the action response, not merely \(TS\). Parattu et al., Equations (111)–(113), derives the area-weighted surface-gravity variation from gravitational momentum variation in its specified static horizon setting. Hopfmüller–Freidel develops the null scalar conjugacy, exact-variation exchange, and corner structure. Odak et al. compares different scalar polarizations explicitly. Those results are foundations, not discoveries of this manuscript.

The membrane comparison is nevertheless not an identity of all pressures. Kolekar–Kothawala's examined passages derive a tangential surface stress and connect its area product to heat content. The manuscript's \(P_L=\Pi/L\) has different dimensions and is the coefficient of a different scale variation. Wang's evolving FLRW membrane construction includes generator/regulator-dependent pressure corrections; it is not the same object as the present instantaneous scalar screen pressure. These additional membrane and phase-space works were discovered during review and must not be attributed to the author's one-page bibliography.

The supplied claim-specific novelty findings therefore support a partly distinctive mechanical interpretation and a distinct FRW screen assignment, with moderate confidence. The search audit includes focused queries and bounded citation neighborhoods, with earlier failed seed lookups subsequently resolved. It is not an exhaustive priority search. An earlier full-text construction using the same length source, action response, and normal-pressure interpretation would change the novelty finding. Conversely, a useful identification need not introduce new dynamics or an experiment to contribute to the field's explanation.

empiricalAssessment.summary: The numbered manuscript presents theoretical identities and a conceptual identification within adopted gravitational frameworks. It reports no observation, experiment, or discriminating testable prediction. Empirical testing is therefore not applicable to the submitted claims, and the absence of new experiments is not a defect.

claimSourceJudgments.reason: The source's area pairing is supported as the prescribed area-response channel: the checked derivative gives \(\Pi\), the full differential retains \(\Pi dA\), and the thermal coefficient gives \(T dS\). Earlier action and membrane passages support the surface-stress interpretation. This does not identify \(\Pi\) with every possible boundary stress tensor.

The force pairs with the scale change as a selected generalized source response, not merely by naming an energy derivative. The supplied restricted action chain gives \(-F_L\delta L\), while Rindler geometry fixes the stated length normalization. The meaning remains clock- and prescription-dependent and does not assert a universal material displacement force.

For a smooth invertible scalar work-coordinate change, transforming the coefficient by the chain rule preserves the same one-form. The supplied kappa-to-length pullback and Schwarzschild length-to-radius transformation are checked instances. This supports the source's work-coordinate statement without asserting invariance under arbitrary changes of action, clock, gauge, or polarization.

On the declared Schwarzschild family, \(L=2R\) and the checked relation \(dL/L=dR/R\) make the two descriptions the same fractional change of horizon size. The transformed force and pressure preserve the work. This does not locate another physical surface at radius 2R or identify areal radius with a universal proper distance.

With energy-density units and the established Einstein–FRW inputs, substituting \(\rho=3P\) yields the printed expansion, acceleration, and conservation equations, including the curved expansion relation. The supplied checks verify those substitutions, and the retrieved cosmological sources establish the underlying Einstein framework. This is an equivalent representation within that framework, not a derivation of its dynamics from the boundary potential alone.

The sum is mathematically checked and coherently interpreted as thermal and horizon-work product representations, each equal to the same U. The supplied companion explicitly excludes independently stored energies. Accordingly, the decomposition language is contextual physical organization of a known mass-energy relation, not a newly proved unique energy partition.

limits: Obligations and exact checks are different counting units: several source assertions may depend on the same check. Counts are not a whole-paper truth percentage or probability.
Source links record traceability, not a machine proof of natural-language interpretation.
Package-level assumptions are listed transparently; a fine-grained dependency is not invented where the approved analysis has not supplied one.
A positive scientific assessment cannot override a contradicted exact expression or supply missing empirical evidence.

The potential-to-work-coordinate inference is conditional on a chosen canonical structure. Algebra alone does not uniquely identify the physical potential, force, clock, boundary/corner terms, or allowed variations.

assumptions.statement: Model 1: The clock normalization is fixed throughout. This is a source premise, not an algebraic conclusion.
Model 1: A and L are independent scalar coordinates for the general response calculation. A derivative with respect to one holds the other fixed; no stationary-radius constraint is imposed.
Model 1: c and G are fixed positive physical constants. pi is the fixed positive dimensionless circle constant, with no rational approximation.
Model 1: The scalar model uses A > 0 and L > 0, excluding degenerate areas and lengths. These explicit domain restrictions supplement the source's stated positive surface gravity.
Model 1: The source relation L = c²/κ is encoded equivalently as κ = c²/L so that L remains an independent differentiation coordinate.

assessment.summary: The supplied excerpts support a polarization-dependent route to an area-weighted surface-gravity variation, but do not establish the manuscript’s complete canonical starting response with its stated normalization, boundary data, corners and sign. The subsequent scalar pullback to acceleration length is supported once that starting response is assumed. The numbered page explicitly imposes a fixed clock, fixed cuts and both \(\theta=0\) and \(\delta\theta=0\); the remaining issue is their implementation and the detailed mixed prescription, not their absence. This is a targeted evidence assessment, not a full proof, physical validation or result for the scalar report.

assessment.summary: The manuscript’s central proposal is a mechanical interpretation of an established gravitational boundary response: use the clock-normalized acceleration length \(L=c^2/\kappa\) as a work coordinate, identify its conjugate force \(F_L=M_U\kappa\), and interpret \(F_L/A\) as a normal-scale pressure. This is more specific than a restatement of \(U=TS\), and it could offer a useful conceptual advance within Einstein gravity. However, earlier supplied passages already derive the same area-weighted surface-gravity variation and its canonical/thermal meaning. The potentially distinctive element is therefore the geometrically motivated length-coordinate interpretation and its pressure/work translations, not the underlying action coefficient. The supplied mathematical report supports the declared scalar identities, but not their operational interpretation, uniqueness, or applicability across physical regimes. The Schwarzschild results are conditional consequences; the FRW construction supplies a different screen-pressure interpretation, not new cosmological dynamics. Overall, the evidence supports a partly distinctive interpretation with substantial prior foundations, while leaving exact priority and the physical status of the proposed force unresolved.

sections.text:
Inputs. The manuscript fixes a clock normalization, assumes positive surface gravity, and adopts the boundary potential
\[
L=\frac{c^2}{\kappa},\qquad U(A,L)=\frac{Ac^2\kappa}{8\pi G}=\frac{c^4A}{8\pi GL}.
\]
Its gravitational origin is an input attributed to the cited boundary prescriptions, not something derived on this page. For the general response calculation, \(A\) and \(L\) are independent coordinates. The force convention is the negative fixed-area length derivative; \(M_U=U/c^2\) is a mass equivalent, not automatically the total gravitational mass.

Construction. Differentiating before imposing any spherical-family constraint gives
\[
dU=\Pi\,dA-F_L\,dL,\qquad
\Pi=\frac{U}{A},\qquad
F_L=\frac{U}{L}=M_U\kappa,
\]
and therefore
\[
P_L=\frac{F_L}{A}=\frac{\Pi}{L}=\frac{\kappa^2}{8\pi G}.
\]
The negative length contribution to \(dU\) must be distinguished from the positive work magnitude \(F_LdL\). Also, \(AL\) is not generally a spherical areal volume.

A second input is the selected scalar action response, under fixed clock and cuts, a specified mixed boundary prescription, and \(\theta=\delta\theta=0\):
\[
\frac{\Theta_\kappa^{(0)}}{\Delta\tau}=\frac{Ac^2}{8\pi G}\delta\kappa.
\]
The coordinate map then gives \(-F_L\delta L\). The scalar transformation is a consequence of this adopted response; establishing that this is the appropriate gravitational response requires the full boundary prescription.

Additional translations. Temperature and area entropy are separately adopted, producing \(U=TS\) and \(\Pi dA=T dS\). Rindler supplies the stated distance interpretation. Schwarzschild imposes \(A=4\pi R^2\), \(L=2R\), and \(U=Mc^2/2\), yielding \(F_R=2F_L=M\kappa\) and \(P_R=2P_L\). A separate instantaneous-equilibrium FRW assignment uses \(L=R_A\), spherical area and volume, and Einstein–Misner–Sharp energy; it yields \(U=E\), \(P=P_L=\rho/3\), and the radius-family identity \(dE=T dS-PdV\).

Check status. An actual report is supplied for package digest 218eb4ef06287c6920a1962a4c70f6133c27e188477b32dc47c18f3d62b0d2ef. Representative checked claims include b1-g01_length_coefficient, b1-g01_mass_acceleration_identity, b1-g01_pressure_surface_gravity, b3-schw_pressure_factor, b4-frw_first_law_radius, and b5-g05_canonical_force_coeff. These have zero scalar residuals and consistent dimensions under their declared premises. They do not independently validate the adopted boundary action, thermal inputs, physical force interpretation, or cosmological applicability.
sections.title: Scientific review — Inputs → construction → claimed outputs

sections.text:
The clearest reading is that the paper gives two mechanical descriptions of changes in a horizon boundary potential. Increasing area at fixed acceleration length increases \(U\), with coefficient \(\Pi\). Increasing acceleration length at fixed area decreases \(U\), with coefficient \(-F_L\). In Rindler geometry, acceleration length has the stated interpretation as the observer’s normal distance to the horizon on an instantaneous rest slice. This motivates treating its variation as a mechanical displacement rather than merely as a change of inverse temperature.

The pressure distinction is essential. \(\Pi\) has units of energy per area, or force per length: it is a two-dimensional surface stress. \(P_L=\Pi/L\) has ordinary three-dimensional pressure units. The proposed normal-scale pressure is not simply another name for membrane surface pressure. Moreover, \(\Pi dA\) and \(A d\Pi=-F_LdL\) are different responses on the independent-coordinate space; one cannot replace area work by length work without specifying which variation is being considered.

Thermal language supplies a useful translation, but is not needed for the derivative-defined force:
\[
\Pi dA=T dS,\qquad A d\Pi=S dT=-F_LdL.
\]
The second relation exposes the closest connection to earlier action calculations: the manuscript proposes a mechanical length-displacement interpretation of the already established area-weighted surface-gravity variation.

The spherical examples require a further distinction between a partial derivative and a derivative along a solution family. For Schwarzschild, area and length co-vary. The complete differential remains the sum of both contributions; \(F_LdL\) alone is not \(dU\). Since \(dL=2dR\) and \(dV=A\,dR\), preserving this work gives \(P_R=2P_L\). The resulting \(Mc^2=TS+F_LL\) consists of two equal products, each \(U\); it does not by itself establish two independently exchangeable energy reservoirs.

For FRW, the length-radius conversion is instead unity, so \(P=P_L\). The identity \(P=\rho/3\) concerns a screen response defined from the assigned geometry and energy. It is not a radiation equation of state for the bulk: the manuscript explicitly keeps bulk pressure \(p_m\) separate. Its acceleration and conservation equations retain that distinction. Evolving FRW is expressly not derived by placing the stationary null-sector response on a stationary worldtube.
sections.title: Scientific review — What the proposal means

sections.text:
The closest precedent is not merely the formula \(TS\). Parattu et al. (2013 preprint, selected passages) derive a horizon surface Hamiltonian with that value and split its variation into a metric contribution and a conjugate-momentum contribution. Their displayed horizon integrals give both \(\kappa\delta A/(8\pi)\) and \(A\delta\kappa/(8\pi)\) in their units. With conventions matched, the latter is precisely the coefficient from which the present manuscript constructs \(-F_L\delta L\). Their variations preserve the near-horizon metric structure and compare horizon configurations; they are not an unrestricted displacement theorem. Thus the action origin, coefficient, and separation of the two response channels have substantial earlier precedent.

Hopfmüller–Freidel (2016 preprint, selected passages) derive the null-boundary action, corner contributions, and spin-zero conjugacy involving area and surface gravity/expansion. They explicitly distinguish a potential containing \(\delta\kappa\) from a polarization in which it is absorbed into an exact variation and the area response. They also hold the boundary location fixed while varying its geometry. These are direct foundations for the manuscript’s canonical interpretation, and demonstrate why action and polarization must be specified.

The 2023 null-charge paper displays several polarizations. In the expansion-free scalar restriction, its CFPk and conformal forms contain \(2\delta k\) times the null measure, whereas its CS form contains \(\delta k\) together with an area-measure variation. Consequently neither nonexpansion alone nor the word “mixed” uniquely determines the manuscript’s coefficient. The supplied passages confirm the relevant response structures, but not the manuscript’s complete prescription.

Earlier membrane calculations obtain surface stresses from a stretched-horizon action variation and a redshift-regulated stress tensor. Kolekar–Kothawala’s 2011 preprint, published in JHEP in 2012, supplies the Einstein-limit relation between membrane surface pressure, area, and horizon heat content. This overlaps \(\Pi\), not automatically the three-dimensional \(P_L\). Its operational source is a membrane stress tensor rather than the inverse-surface-gravity displacement proposed here.

Cosmological horizon thermodynamics also predates this manuscript. Cai–Kim (2005) derive Friedmann equations using apparent-horizon heat flux and an inverse-radius equilibrium temperature assignment, with an explicit dynamical-horizon qualification. Akbar–Cai (2006 preprint) use \(E=\rho V\) and a moving apparent horizon to obtain \(dE=T dS+WdV\), with \(W=(\rho-p_m)/2\). This is not the same pressure coefficient as the manuscript’s \(P=\rho/3\). Wang’s 2014 preprint additionally treats FLRW membrane pressure and cosmological equations, including a time-dependent regulator correction.
sections.title: Scientific review — Established foundations and direct overlaps

sections.text:
The strongest candidate advance is the identification of \(L=c^2/\kappa\) as a geometrically motivated mechanical coordinate, with an action-supported conjugate force and a normal-scale force density. This should not be dismissed simply because it introduces neither a new interaction nor new Einstein equations. If an admissible geometric variation and an operational response can be specified, recognizing an existing canonical response as length work could change how horizon mechanics is interpreted.

The distinction must nevertheless be narrow. Parattu et al. already derive the same area-weighted \(\delta\kappa\) coefficient from a gravitational momentum variation, not just from multiplying temperature and entropy. Hopfmüller–Freidel and the 2023 null-charge paper already explain the underlying conjugacy and polarization dependence. The manuscript adds the inverse-surface-gravity coordinate map, its Rindler distance motivation, and the force/pressure identification. On the supplied passages this is a partly distinctive interpretation of an earlier response, not a newly discovered action term or an additional canonical degree of freedom. Those excerpts do not establish whether the same length interpretation occurs elsewhere in the complete papers or wider literature.

The critical physical question is what \(\delta L\) represents. The prior null-boundary calculations vary geometry on a fixed boundary. The manuscript describes horizon-scale change, but has not supplied a general construction showing when this parameter variation is a measurable normal displacement while preserving its clock, cuts, and allowed variations. Rindler gives its best local geometric motivation. Schwarzschild’s \(L=2R\), with time normalized at infinity, is a scale relation rather than a claim that \(L\) is a proper radial distance. Comparing these meanings is necessary before asserting a common mechanical operation.

The Schwarzschild factor \(P_R/P_L=2\) is a sound conditional consequence of the chosen coordinate conversion. Its explanatory interest is that work is preserved while force and pressure coefficients change. The mass-energy sum adds a mechanical reading to two equal products, but no independent partition or new first law is established.

The FRW pressure is a second potentially useful interpretation: it connects the assigned normal-scale force to \(P=\rho/3\), distinct from both bulk pressure and Akbar–Cai work density. This differs substantively in coefficient, temperature prescription, and response interpretation. It must be presented as a separate equilibrium-screen construction, not as confirmation of the full dynamical unified first law or of Wang’s membrane stress.

No new testable empirical prediction is supplied. The force and pressure coefficients are theoretical consistency targets conditional on the adopted prescriptions. The printed cosmological equations are explicitly Einstein–FRW equations in new variables, so their agreement with observations would not discriminate this interpretation from Einstein gravity.
sections.title: Scientific review — Precisely what might advance the subject

sections.text:
Established layer. The supplied literature already connects gravitational boundary actions, area/surface-gravity conjugacy, membrane stresses, horizon heat content, and apparent-horizon cosmology. The manuscript does not replace those explanations or derive their foundations anew.

Proposed layer. Its most useful contribution could be a precise bridge between the canonical surface-gravity response and a length-work description. In that bridge, \(\Pi\) describes an area response, \(F_L\) a normal-scale response, and \(P_L\) its force per area. Keeping these quantities distinct could clarify why different horizon “pressures” have different dimensions and coefficients. The Schwarzschild and FRW examples make a concrete point: choosing \(L=2R\) versus \(L=R_A\) changes radial work coefficients without changing the work itself. That is a potentially valuable conceptual clarification, rather than evidence for an extra interaction.

The advance remains conditional on showing that the geometrically normalized coordinate is physically privileged for the stated response, not just convenient. Existing action/polarization analyses make this a substantive requirement. If established, the proposal would enrich the mechanical interpretation of a known sector of Einstein gravity. It would not increase the number of boundary degrees of freedom or alter the bulk equations.

The cosmological payoff is currently interpretive. \(P=\rho/3\) offers a screen-response variable while \(p_m\) continues to control the matter contribution to acceleration and conservation. This could help organize comparisons between equilibrium-screen mechanics and dynamical horizon thermodynamics, but does not explain a new source of cosmic acceleration, determine vacuum energy, or supply a new matter equation of state.

Speculative extensions—such as an independently measurable horizon force, a unique physical energy partition, or applications to general evolving boundaries—are not established here. No new observational prediction is provided. The field contribution should therefore be framed as a bounded, potentially insightful mechanical identification with checked scalar consequences, not as demonstrated new gravitational dynamics or certified originality.
sections.title: Scientific review — Explanatory value and wider contribution

sections.text:
1. Boundary prescription and coefficient. The page does not provide the complete bulk/boundary/corner action, orientation conventions, normalization of the null measure, or exact polarization defining its “mixed” prescription. The displayed earlier polarizations differ in their \(\delta k\) and area terms. A derivation must show which prescription yields the printed coefficient and what is retained or removed by exact variations and corners. The scalar restriction must also explain how shear and generator-variation sectors are excluded. Harlow–Wu, the relative-bicomplex treatment, and the null-boundary analyses show why these details matter; a scalar coefficient match is not a complete covariant-phase-space derivation.

2. Admissible displacement and clock dependence. Independent \(A,L\) variations are useful for the potential calculation, but their realization by allowed metric variations requires demonstration. A fixed boundary with varying geometry is not automatically a displaced boundary. Rindler’s distance interpretation does not remove observer/time-normalization dependence for arbitrary horizons. The force and pressure should remain explicitly attached to their clock and boundary prescription.

3. Physical interpretation. Differentiating the adopted potential establishes a generalized response by definition, not a measured stress or a new force law. Likewise, \(U=TS\) does not automatically make \(U\) an internal energy for every thermodynamic process. The Schwarzschild sum requires an independent physical accounting argument if it is intended as more than two equal products adding to the stipulated mass energy.

4. Evolving FRW. The page appropriately separates its instantaneous screen assignment from the stationary null sector. Nevertheless, the range of validity of its positive inverse-radius temperature and \(L=R_A\) assignment is not quantified. Cai–Kim discuss the approximation involved in a dynamical apparent-horizon temperature; Akbar–Cai use a different work density and surface-gravity prescription; Wang finds a dynamical membrane-pressure correction. These cannot be identified with the manuscript’s \(P\) without an explicit translation. The scalar first-law identity does not derive the acceleration or conservation laws from the boundary potential.

5. Mathematical report. All listed report claims have status checked; no contradicted or inconclusive cases are reported. This covers only the declared scalar models and domains. For example, b3-potential_length_substitution is explicitly a definition-restatement. Claims b4-frw_acceleration_coefficient_rewrite and b4-frw_conservation_expression_rewrite check substitutions, not independent cosmological evolution laws. Claim b5-g05_canonical_force_coeff checks a coordinate transformation of an adopted coefficient, not the full canonical one-form. The report is not empirical validation or approval of the manuscript.

6. Source and literature scope. Only the numbered one-page manuscript is available; its companion manuscripts are not supplied. Literature evidence consists of selected excerpts or abstracts, not complete readings. Some excerpts are truncated. The assessed 2201.12141 record has a thesis-like abstract inconsistent with its article title, so its selected article passages are the safer basis. The Mongan hit remains abstract-level and irrelevant to the exact force claim. The finite search and bounded citation neighborhoods do not establish exhaustive priority. The audit has no currently unresolved unavailable requests; the earlier failed seed lookups were subsequently successful.

7. Chronology. The sole present-date reference is 2026-10-26T00:36:50.473Z. The manuscript’s explicit date, 22 October 2026, is not future-dated. The July 2026 quantum-membrane record also predates this assessment and manuscript. No assessed record has an explicit date later than the assessment timestamp. Preprint chronology must not be replaced by later journal dates: examples include the 2011 membrane preprint published in JHEP in 2012 and Harlow–Wu’s 2019 preprint published in JHEP in 2020. Where exact version or publication dates are not supplied, detailed priority remains uncertain.

comparisons.proposedDifference: The manuscript holds a clock fixed and gives meaning to a varying surface gravity through \(L\). Its response is not the same operation as extracting a stretched-horizon stress tensor in a gauge with \(\delta\kappa=0\).

comparisons.proposedDifference: The manuscript works with a scalar boundary potential and a length-conjugate response, not the full fluid stress tensor or transport coefficients. The shared action-based motivation is relevant, but does not show equality of the pressures.

neededEvidence: Full-text comparison of embedding variations and geometric parameter variations.

comparisons.proposedDifference: The manuscript fixes cuts in its canonical statement but speaks of horizon-scale change. A fluctuating-boundary construction could clarify whether its mechanical displacement changes embedding or only boundary geometry, but the abstract does not resolve this.

neededEvidence: Full-text comparison only if an extended-thermodynamic interpretation is claimed.

comparisons.proposedDifference: The manuscript’s \(L\) is inverse surface gravity at fixed gravitational constants, not a coupling-derived length varied in extended thermodynamics. The abstract supports this broad distinction, not a detailed priority finding.

comparisons.alreadyKnown: Selected full-text passages propose a microscopic quantum membrane with charged horizon degrees of freedom and frequency- and helicity-dependent electromagnetic response. The supplied record is dated July 2026, before this manuscript and assessment.

limitations: This is a disclosed bounded search of arXiv, Crossref and INSPIRE, not an exhaustive literature search or proof of novelty, priority, physical correctness, or empirical validity.

Discovery records provide metadata and available abstracts. Cited and up to six discovered sources may supply selected primary passages, registered by source hash and locator; no complete reading of those papers is claimed. Detailed equivalence still depends on the exact compared claims and conventions.

Initial search uses up to five focused queries with six results per provider. Up to three validated INSPIRE seeds add six references and six citing records each; at most one alternative-query round is used. The complete bounded discovery registry is retained, while up to 24 deduplicated papers are synthesized.
Search and model outputs can contain mistakes. Proposed advances and field contributions remain conditional until the underlying claims and prior-art comparisons are independently supported.
Original approval, equation-check reports, canonical assessments, and published explanations are preserved; this supplement does not change their scientific status.

review.summary: The supplied one-page manuscript reorganizes an adopted Einstein boundary potential using acceleration length L = c²/κ. It develops derivative-defined force and force density, connects them to thermal products and stationary-horizon work, applies a separate equilibrium-screen assignment to FRW, and quotes a restricted canonical response as its physical basis. The supplied report marks all 51 selected scalar checks as checked, with zero exact residuals, consistent dimensions, and established domain obligations. This supports the selected conditional algebra, not validation of the whole paper or its physical foundations.
review.priorWork: No literature-wide novelty search or independent source verification was performed by this pipeline. The source attributes the boundary prescription and canonical response to Hopfmüller–Freidel (1611.03096), Odak et al. (2309.03854), and Parattu et al. (1303.1535). It invokes Cai–Kim (hep-th/0501055) and Akbar–Cai (hep-th/0609128) for the cosmological energy identification, and refers to companion seven-page and full manuscripts for details and scope. These attributions are retained as source citations only: the cited works and companions were not independently read here, their adequacy was not established, and no priority or novelty conclusion follows.
strengths: The selected scalar derivatives, products, work transformations, and thermal comparisons are internally consistent under the declared premises.
The minus sign in the length contribution to dU is kept distinct from positive horizon work.
Independent-coordinate mechanics, Schwarzschild family calculations, and instantaneous-equilibrium FRW calculations are separated rather than silently mixed.
The source offers a restricted action-response argument for the physical interpretation instead of relying only on an energy-derivative definition.
The distinction between screen pressure and total bulk pressure prevents P = ρ/3 from being misread as a bulk-matter equation of state.
review.correctness: 51/51 selected mathematical candidates returned checked. 3 source coverage units remain unresolved. Definition restatements are not independent derivations. No mathematical contradiction is reported for any exact tested expression on its declared domain. The calculations preserve the essential ordering: independent-coordinate derivatives precede Schwarzschild family restriction, while subsequent family derivatives vary the radius. The FRW batch explicitly adopts its length-work coefficient rather than deriving it from a radius-constrained fixed-area derivative. Its spherical-area relation, energy-density reading, positive domains, and ordinary derivative-coefficient interpretation remain disclosed translation premises requiring source-fidelity assessment. One potential rewrite is classified as a definition restatement. The broader c023, c096, and c097 coverage units retain unsupported status even though their selected ratio or coefficient subclaims succeed; that is not evidence of a manuscript error. Full tensor equations, field-space variations, square-root branches, and cosmological dynamics were not checked.

review.recommendation: Proceed to source-aware expert review of the physical and canonical foundations, using the successful scalar checks as bounded supporting evidence. Confirm the transcription and inferred premises, inspect the cited and companion derivations, and keep the distinction between conditional identities, adopted physical laws, and interpretations explicit. These results do not call for a mathematical correction to the tested expressions, but they are insufficient for an overall validity or novelty judgment.
review.physicalJustification: The listed physical inputs are adopted premises, not established by these algebraic checks. The source supplies or cites several substantive foundations: the Einstein boundary prescription for U; a Rindler normal-distance interpretation for L; infinity-normalized Schwarzschild family assignments; Hawking–Unruh temperature and area entropy; the Einstein–Misner–Sharp energy identification; and a canonical response restricted by fixed clock, cuts, mixed boundary data, and θ = δθ = 0. It expressly separates evolving FRW screens from the stationary canonical sector and says no new interaction is introduced. The tool checked scalar consequences and coefficient transformations, not those foundations themselves. Further assessment should inspect the cited boundary/action derivation and its conventions, the admissible variations and canonical normalization, the geometric distance identification, the stationary-sector realizations, and the applicability of instantaneous equilibrium to the cosmological assignment. Full Einstein–FRW translation also needs assessment with the stated energy-density, bulk-pressure, curvature, and vacuum conventions. No independent empirical evidence was evaluated. A conditional reformulation within accepted GR does not inherently require a new experiment; any additional empirical claim would need specified predictions and relevant independent evidence.
review.explanatoryContribution: The clearest contribution is the organization of boundary responses around a length coordinate and the separation of area response, length work, and coordinate-transformed pressure. The Schwarzschild factor P_R = 2P_L versus the FRW equality P = P_L makes the role of work-coordinate normalization especially concrete. The thermal and mass-energy products provide a compact synthesis, but their algebraic equality does not by itself establish a unique physical energy partition. Whether this organization or its interpretation is new cannot be determined from the supplied checks.

explanation.text: The construction starts with a fixed clock normalization, positive surface gravity κ, horizon area A, and acceleration length L = c²/κ. It adopts the boundary potential U = Aκc²/(8πG), attributed in the source to a specified Einstein boundary prescription. Substitution gives U = c⁴A/(8πGL), which the checker confirms algebraically. This separates two questions: the substitution is checked, while the gravitational justification of the adopted potential remains a cited physical input. The general scalar model treats A and L as independent positive coordinates, with the physical constants fixed.
explanation.title: Starting point: a prescribed boundary potential

explanation.text: The area response is defined as Π = (∂U/∂A) at fixed L; the length response is defined as F_L = −(∂U/∂L) at fixed A. The checked derivatives give Π = c⁴/(8πGL) and F_L = Ac⁴/(8πGL²), hence dU = Π dA − F_L dL. Increasing area at fixed length raises U, whereas increasing length at fixed area lowers it. The positive work quantity F_L dL must therefore not be confused with the complete change in U. These calculations use neither temperature nor entropy, supporting the source's construction-level thermal-independence statement. Calling the coefficients physical surface stress and generalized force additionally invokes the source's boundary-mechanical interpretation.
explanation.title: Two responses, with an important sign distinction

explanation.text: The checked consequences are Π = U/A and F_L = U/L. With the adopted mass equivalent M_U = U/c², this also gives F_L = M_Uκ. That resemblance to mass times acceleration is a scalar identity within this model, not an independently established force law. Defining force density by P_L = F_L/A gives P_L = Π/L = κ²/(8πG). The products U = ΠA = F_LL = P_LAL are all checked representations of the same potential; they do not identify separate energy stores, and AL is not automatically a spherical volume. Finally, Π has no area dependence at fixed L, and A(∂Π/∂L) = −F_L. Together these checked coefficients give A dΠ = −F_L dL in the independent-coordinate model.
explanation.title: Force density and related mechanical identities

explanation.text: The source separately adopts the Hawking–Unruh temperature T = ℏc/(2πk_BL), the area entropy S = k_BA/(4ℓ_P²), and ℓ_P² = ℏG/c³. Their product simplifies to U; this comparison is checked, but does not derive either thermal prescription from mechanics. Differentiating the adopted entropy gives (∂S/∂A)_L = k_B/(4ℓ_P²) and (∂S/∂L)_A = 0. The checked equality T(∂S/∂A)_L = Π then supplies both scalar coefficients of Π dA = T dS. The distinction matters: U = TS is a product identity, while Π dA = T dS translates an area response. Multiplying T by dS does not differentiate the product TS.
explanation.title: Thermal translation uses additional physical inputs

explanation.text: The source's geometric argument is the stated Rindler identification: L = c²/a_obs is the normal horizon distance on the observer's instantaneous rest slice, with planar patch area independent of L. This is the proposed reason for treating L as a geometrically normalized work coordinate, rather than merely an algebraic inverse of κ. The scalar checker did not reproduce the metric, observer, or slice construction needed to assess that identification. Likewise, the source states that other coordinates preserve work when their coefficients transform. The Schwarzschild and canonical calculations below test particular scalar transformations, not a general geometric work-invariance theorem.
explanation.title: What supplies the proposed geometric normalization?

explanation.text: For the adopted Schwarzschild family, A = 4πR², L = 2R, U = Mc²/2, and V = 4πR³/3, with time normalized at infinity. The mechanical length derivative is taken before imposing these family relations. Along the family, the positive-work convention gives F_R = F_L(dL/dR) = 2F_L. The checked identities give F_R = Mκ = c⁴/(4G) and P_R(dV/dR) = Mκ. Since dV/dR equals the spherical area, the transformed pressure is P_R = 2P_L = κ²/(4πG). Thus the factor of two reflects the chosen length-radius conversion, not conflicting universal pressure formulas. The checker also confirms dL/L = dR/R. Area and volume co-vary here; they are not additional independent family coordinates, and this positive work chain is not the full differential of U.
explanation.title: Schwarzschild: changing work coordinate produces a factor of two

explanation.text: The checked family-specific identities are U = 3P_RV and TS = F_LL = U. Together with the adopted normalization U = Mc²/2, they yield Mc² = TS + F_LL: each product equals half the mass energy. The algebraic sum is checked; its interpretation as a physical mass-energy decomposition is a further interpretive claim, not proof that the two terms are independently stored energies or that this partition is unique. Separately, the checker verifies c²(dM/dR) = T(dS/dR), the radius coefficient of d(Mc²) = T dS. Since Mc² = 2U throughout this family, that mass first law must not be substituted for a claim that dU = T dS along the same family.
explanation.title: Schwarzschild energy products and the mass first law

explanation.text: The cosmological application explicitly uses an instantaneous-equilibrium screen, not a stationary worldtube. It adopts L = R_A and V = 4πR_A³/3. The formal translation additionally makes explicit the inferred spherical-area premise A = 4πR_A² and reads ρ = E/V as energy density. Under these assumptions, the boundary potential matches the independently prescribed expression E = c⁴R_A/(2G). The scalar comparison is checked; the physical Einstein–Misner–Sharp identification is attributed to reference [2], not established by that comparison. Because dL/dR_A = 1, the work transformation gives P = P_L rather than the Schwarzschild factor of two. The checker confirms P = ρ/3 and the radius coefficient of dE = T dS − P dV. This is a screen-pressure relation, not a bulk-matter equation of state.
explanation.title: FRW screens use a separate equilibrium assignment

explanation.text: With κ_E = 8πG/c⁴, the checked screen relation is 1/R_A² = κ_EP. Substituting the adopted flat-radius relation R_A = c/H on the positive expanding branch gives H² = (8πG/c²)P. The curved counterpart, H² + kc²/a² = (8πG/c²)P, was checked after solving the adopted squared-radius relation for k; that calculation neither independently establishes the geometric radius prescription nor proves its square-root branch. Using ρ = 3P, the checker also confirms −(κ_E/3)(ρ + 3p_m) = −κ_E(P + p_m) and [ρ̇ + 3H(ρ + p_m)]/3 = Ṗ + H(3P + p_m). The latter uses an instantaneous chain-rule representation through an arbitrary radial rate. No scale-factor acceleration was calculated, and neither conservation expression was proved to vanish. The full Einstein–FRW interpretation therefore remains conditional on the gravitational equations and physical identifications. The source explicitly distinguishes total bulk pressure p_m from screen pressure P; its stated consistent inclusion of vacuum contributions was not independently tracked.
explanation.title: Cosmological rewrites are conditional, not new dynamics

explanation.text: The force interpretation is not presented solely as an energy derivative. The source quotes and cites an action-level scalar response Θ_κ^(0)/Δτ = [Ac²/(8πG)]δκ, restricted to a fixed clock, fixed cuts, the stated mixed boundary prescription, and θ = δθ = 0. The checker confirms dκ/dL = −c²/L² and the coefficient transformation [Ac²/(8πG)](dκ/dL) = −Ac⁴/(8πGL²) = −F_L. Thus, conditional on the quoted canonical response and admissible coordinate variation, the transformed coefficient matches the mechanical force. The full canonical one-form, its action origin, normalization, and allowed variations were not reproduced by this scalar tool. claims.title: Acceleration-length substitution in the potential
claims.explanation: Candidate substitution check for c015: insert the adopted κ = c²/L into the separately adopted potential Aκc²/(8πG). This does not independently justify either physical input.

claims.title: Fixed-length area coefficient of dU
claims.explanation: Candidate explicit area derivative at fixed L. It addresses c116 and only the dA coefficient of c017 and c018. In c018 the coefficient is named Pi by its adopted derivative definition; the length coefficient is addressed separately.

claims.title: Fixed-area length coefficient of dU
claims.explanation: Candidate explicit length derivative at fixed A, including the L-dependence of κ. It addresses c117 and only the dL coefficient of c017 and c018. The adopted sign convention identifies this coefficient with −F_L.

claims.title: Area response equals potential per area
claims.explanation: Candidate comparison of the adopted fixed-L derivative with U/A. Positive A makes the quotient defined. The equality U/A is not imposed in the definition of Pi.

claims.title: Length response equals potential per length
claims.explanation: Candidate comparison of the negative fixed-A derivative with U/L. The equality U/L is not imposed in the definition of F_L.

claims.title: Length response and mass-equivalent acceleration
claims.explanation: Candidate scalar identity comparing the derivative-defined F_L with (U/c²)κ using the adopted acceleration-length normalization. It does not establish an independent inertial or gravitational force law.

claims.title: Force density equals area response per length
claims.explanation: Candidate comparison of the adopted force density F_L/A with Pi/L. Both response coefficients retain their derivative definitions.

claims.title: Force density in surface-gravity variables
claims.explanation: Candidate comparison of derivative-defined force per area with κ²/(8πG), using κ = c²/L. This formula is not adopted as the definition of P_L.

claims.title: Potential as area response times area
claims.explanation: Candidate product identity using Pi defined by differentiation, not by U/A. This addresses only the U = Pi A equality in the printed product chain.

claims.title: Potential as length response times length
claims.explanation: Candidate product identity using F_L defined by the negative length derivative, not by U/L. This addresses only the U = F_L L equality in the printed product chain.

claims.title: Vanishing area derivative of the area response
claims.explanation: Candidate nested-derivative computation for c118. In A dPi = −F_L dL, the dA coefficient is A(∂Pi/∂A)_L = 0. Because A is positive, the displayed candidate is its equivalent divided form. This covers only the dA coefficient of c033.

claims.title: Length coefficient of the stress-work relation
claims.explanation: Candidate derivative comparison for c119. It addresses the dL coefficient of c033, A(∂Pi/∂L)_A = −F_L, separately from the vanishing dA coefficient.

claims.title: Acceleration-length substitution in the adopted potential
claims.explanation: This candidate substitutes the disclosed kappa = c^2/L definition into the adopted boundary potential. Coverage c014 is represented as an input definition, not independently verified; the algebraic target is c015.

claims.title: Evaluate the fixed-length area derivative
claims.explanation: The candidate evaluates the derivative used to define Pi in c020. A and L remain independent, so L and therefore kappa(L) are fixed during this area derivative.

claims.title: Evaluate the negative fixed-area length derivative
claims.explanation: This candidate evaluates the derivative defining F_L in c022, including its stipulated minus sign. The derivative follows the encoded kappa(L) dependence and holds A fixed; it uses no thermal prescription.

claims.title: Expand the adopted force-density definition
claims.explanation: For c025, the candidate expands P_L = F_L/A and the derivative definition of F_L, then cancels the nonzero area. It computes the scalar density without independently establishing its pressure interpretation.

claims.title: Compare the potential with the pressure-length-area product
claims.explanation: This candidate compares the independently defined potential and mechanical force-density product for c030. It uses only the potential, acceleration-length prescription and response definitions; A L is not treated as an areal volume.

claims.title: Compare the independently stipulated thermal product with U
claims.explanation: The candidate multiplies the separately stipulated temperature and entropy, substitutes the Planck-area definition, and compares the result with U. Coverage c037, c038 and c039 is supplied only through disclosed adopted definitions; the derived equality target is c040. This is not a test of the physical temperature or entropy laws.

claims.title: Differentiate the stipulated entropy with respect to area
claims.explanation: For c120, this candidate differentiates the supplied linear area-entropy law at fixed L and fixed constants. The entropy law itself remains an adopted physical premise.

claims.title: Match the area coefficient of the thermal work identity
claims.explanation: This candidate compares T times the entropy area derivative with the mechanical area derivative Pi. It targets c121 and only the dA coefficient of c041. The temperature is a multiplier in T dS; this is not a derivative of T S.

claims.title: Evaluate the remaining independent-coordinate entropy derivative
claims.explanation: This candidate targets c122 by differentiating S at fixed A. For the dL coefficient of c041, Pi dA has zero coefficient and T dS has coefficient T times this derivative. With finite T on the stated domain, the proposed zero derivative supplies that second scalar coefficient match.

claims.title: Eliminate surface gravity in the independent-coordinate potential
claims.explanation: The left expression is the adopted potential after the explicit substitution kappa = c^2/L_free; multiplying its two c^2 factors gives the right expression. This candidate covers the algebraic assertion c015 before any family restriction. c013 and c014 are encoded inputs to that substitution, not independently established physical relations.

claims.title: Radius-work coefficient has the Schwarzschild factor two
claims.explanation: Compute d(2*R)/dR = 2 in the adopted work transformation F_R = F_L*(dL/dR). This is the scalar coefficient of c050 and directly targets c123. The area and length assignments c045 and c046 are family premises; the work transformation is a convention, not independent physical evidence.

claims.title: Radius-work coefficient equals mass times surface gravity
claims.explanation: The adopted potential and family relations give U = c^4*R/(4*G), hence the adopted mass normalization gives M = c^2*R/(2*G). The fixed-area response followed by the family substitution gives F_L = c^4/(8*G), and dL/dR = 2. Thus the proposed two sides reduce to c^4/(4*G). This is the scalar coefficient of c051 and the explicit target c124; c047 is the disclosed mass input.

claims.title: Pressure-volume work coefficient equals mass times surface gravity
claims.explanation: Differentiate V = 4*pi*R^3/3 to obtain dV/dR = 4*pi*R^2. With the adopted transformed work coefficient, P_R = c^4/(16*pi*G*R^2), so the left expression reduces to c^4/(4*G), as does M*kappa. This targets c125 and the scalar content of c052. c049 is an adopted volume definition. For c057, coverage is the encoded common-radius family dependence of A and V, not a separate geometric derivation.

claims.title: Areal-volume pressure is twice normal-scale force density
claims.explanation: The definitions give P_R = F_L*(dL/dR)/(dV/dR), while P_L = F_L/A. Substituting dL/dR = 2, dV/dR = 4*pi*R^2, and A = 4*pi*R^2 yields the proposed factor two. c025 is the adopted force-density convention; c053 is the candidate consequence. Together with schw_pressure_kappa, this also supplies the stated P_L formula c027.

claims.title: Areal-volume pressure in surface-gravity variables
claims.explanation: The transformed pressure expression is c^4/(16*pi*G*R^2). Substituting kappa = c^2/(2*R) into the right expression gives that same expression. This directly targets c054. Combined with schw_pressure_factor, it implies c027, P_L = kappa^2/(8*pi*G); that implication is not a separate candidate equality.

claims.title: Fractional length and radius displacement coefficients agree
claims.explanation: Differentiate the adopted L = 2*R before dividing by L. The resulting coefficient is 2/(2*R) = 1/R on R > 0. This targets c126 and is the scalar derivative-coefficient translation of c055, not a proof of the geometric interpretation of the displacement.

claims.title: Boundary potential equals three times radial pressure-volume product
claims.explanation: From the adopted potential, U = c^4*R/(4*G). Substituting the independently transformed pressure and the areal volume into 3*P_R*V gives 3*[c^4/(16*pi*G*R^2)]*[4*pi*R^3/3] = c^4*R/(4*G). This is the family-specific product target c058.

claims.title: Mass energy equals the thermal and length-work sum
claims.explanation: The adopted mass normalization gives M*c^2 = c^4*R/(2*G). Separate substitutions into the thermal and work products give c^4*R/(4*G) for each term, whose sum is the left expression. This targets the algebraic sum c059 only; it does not establish a unique physical decomposition of mass energy.

claims.title: Thermal product equals the boundary potential
claims.explanation: The adopted thermal inputs give T = hbar*c/(4*pi*kB*R) and S = pi*kB*c^3*R^2/(hbar*G). Their product reduces to c^4*R/(4*G), the expression obtained separately from the prescribed potential. This targets c060. c037, c038, and c039 are the disclosed temperature, entropy, and Planck-area inputs, not independently established laws.

claims.title: Length-work product equals the boundary potential
claims.explanation: The fixed-area derivative gives F_L = c^4/(8*G) after the family substitution. Multiplication by L = 2*R gives c^4*R/(4*G), matching the separately defined potential. This targets c061. Because L > 0, this product equality is also equivalent to the family restriction of c023, F_L = U/L.

claims.title: Total-radius coefficient of the Schwarzschild mass first law
claims.explanation: Determine M = c^2*R/(2*G) from the adopted potential and mass normalization before differentiation, giving c^2*dM/dR = c^4/(2*G). Independently, S = pi*kB*c^3*R^2/(hbar*G) gives dS/dR = 2*pi*kB*c^3*R/(hbar*G); multiplication by T = hbar*c/(4*pi*kB*R) gives c^4/(2*G). This targets c127 and the scalar total-family coefficient of c062, not the independent-coordinate differential of U.

claims.title: Acceleration-length substitution in the potential
claims.explanation: Candidate substitution check for c015 within the chosen family: replace kappa by c^2/L in the separately adopted A*kappa*c^2 potential. This does not establish the boundary prescription.

claims.title: Normal-scale pressure in surface-gravity variables
claims.explanation: Candidate equality comparing the adopted force-per-area definition with the surface-gravity expression after applying kappa = c^2/L. It covers the scalar pressure formula, not its gravitational interpretation.

claims.title: Unit length-radius conversion gives P = P_L
claims.explanation: Candidate comparison of radial-work pressure with normal force density. The P definition differentiates L = R_A and uses dV/dR_A = 4*pi*R_A^2; the inferred spherical area then supplies the same denominator as F_L/A. This is a scalar work-coefficient check, not an assumed identification.

claims.title: Screen pressure is one third of screen energy density
claims.explanation: Candidate comparison of the radial-work pressure with E/(3*V), using the independently adopted energy and volume formulas. This is not an equation of state for p_m.

claims.title: Radius coefficient of the equilibrium-screen first law
claims.explanation: Candidate ordinary-derivative translation of dE = T*dS - P*dV along the independent radius. It differentiates the independently specified E, entropy and volume formulas at fixed constants. Coverage is the one-parameter scalar coefficient only.

claims.title: Potential evaluated on the spherical FRW screen
claims.explanation: Candidate comparison between U defined from the boundary potential and E independently defined as c^4*R_A/(2*G). Expanding A = 4*pi*R_A^2, L = R_A and kappa = c^2/L makes this the requested potential-substitution calculation. It does not prove the cited Einstein–Misner–Sharp identification.

claims.title: Conditional flat-screen expansion expression
claims.explanation: Candidate flat-family algebra using the explicit substitution H = c/R_A. The pressure is obtained from the work definitions, not from an adopted expansion law. This addresses conditional consistency c130, not the independent gravitational assertion c077.

claims.title: Density substitution in the acceleration coefficient
claims.explanation: Candidate algebraic rewrite of -(kappa_E/3)*(rho + 3*p_m) using the screen-density assignment. No acceleration, scale-factor evolution or Einstein acceleration law is inferred.

claims.title: Chain-rule rewrite of the conservation expression
claims.explanation: Candidate exact scalar rewrite with rho-dot represented by v_R*diff(rho,R_A), and P-dot likewise. H, p_m and v_R are arbitrary instantaneous scalars within their disclosed domains. Neither side is asserted to vanish, and no general time-dependent function or dynamical law is encoded.

claims.title: Squared curved-radius input under a rational parametrization
claims.explanation: Candidate substitution calculation for the squared curved-radius relation. The substitution solves the supplied squared relation for k, so this checks the arithmetic of that parametrization only; it is not independent evidence for the radius prescription and does not establish a square-root branch.

claims.title: Conditional curved-screen expansion expression
claims.explanation: Candidate combination of the adopted squared-radius parametrization with the separately defined screen pressure. Unlike the squared-radius arithmetic alone, this compares the geometric expression with the work-pressure expression. It remains conditional algebra, not an Einstein-equation derivation.

claims.title: Inverse-radius screen-pressure relation
claims.explanation: Candidate scalar equality obtained by comparing the inverse squared radius with the independently defined coupling times radial-work pressure. This does not require the curved-radius prescription or any evolution law.

claims.title: Recover the stated length normalization
claims.explanation: This candidate records the algebraic inverse of the adopted definition κ(L) = c²/L on the positive domain. It restates the source normalization and is not an independent verification of its geometric or physical meaning.

claims.title: Express the adopted potential in independent A and L
claims.explanation: Substitute the independently disclosed coordinate definition κ = c²/L into the adopted potential U = Aκc²/(8πG). The candidate concerns the displayed algebraic equivalence, not the gravitational justification for the potential.

claims.title: Compare the derivative-defined force with U/L
claims.explanation: Expand F_L as −∂U/∂L at fixed independent A, differentiate the adopted potential with κ(L) substituted, and compare the result with U/L. The force-ratio conclusion is not included in the definition of F_L.

claims.title: Differentiate the surface-gravity coordinate map
claims.explanation: Differentiate the adopted κ(L) = c²/L with fixed c. This is the scalar coordinate derivative required for converting the quoted δκ coefficient into a δL coefficient.

claims.title: Transform the cited canonical coefficient to L
claims.explanation: Multiply the adopted coefficient Ac²/(8πG) by dκ/dL. This candidate covers c136 and only the scalar δL coefficient in c096; it does not establish the starting canonical response or its admissible variations.

claims.title: Compare the transformed canonical coefficient with minus the force
claims.explanation: Compare the coordinate-transformed coefficient of the separately adopted canonical input with minus the force defined by differentiating U at fixed A. This candidate covers c137 and the scalar coefficient identification in c097, not the action origin or physical interpretation of the response.

Adopt c022: F_L is minus the partial derivative of U with respect to independent length L, holding A and the constants fixed. No temperature or entropy prescription enters this definition.

Adopt c039, ell_P^2 = hbar G/c^3. The symbol denotes the squared Planck length directly, avoiding any square-root convention; it is fixed under both partial derivatives.

consequences.text: Together, the two proposed coefficient equalities would reproduce the explicit dA and dL terms of c017. With the adopted response definitions, they also give the scalar coefficient reading of c018, dU = Pi dA − F_L dL.
consequences.title: Complete differential in the independent-coordinate model

consequences.text: Together, the proposed area and length derivative equalities would give both coefficients of A dPi = −F_L dL on the stated independent-(A,L) domain.
consequences.title: Scalar content of the stress-work relation

consequences.text: The proposed product equalities would identify Pi A and F_L L with the same adopted boundary potential. They do not independently establish the physical interpretation of either response.
consequences.title: Two mechanical product representations

consequences.text: The proposed U = T S comparison is conditional on three separately disclosed thermal inputs: the temperature prescription, area-entropy law and Planck-area convention. It does not derive those inputs from mechanics.
consequences.title: Conditional thermal energy identity

consequences.text: The area-coefficient candidate and zero length-derivative candidate together represent Pi dA = T dS for independent scalar variations of A and L. Their scope is ordinary coordinate coefficients, not a covariant differential-form theorem.
consequences.title: Two scalar coefficients of the thermal differential identity

consequences.text: The displayed definitions and proposed force and density computations depend on A, L, c, G and pi, but not on T, S, hbar or kB. This records the construction-level content of the source's thermal-independence statements without asserting physical applicability beyond the adopted boundary model.
consequences.title: Mechanical dependency scope

consequences.text: The proposed U = P_L A L identity concerns the geometric product A L only. It supplies no identification of that product with a spherical areal volume.
consequences.title: Pressure product without a volume identification

consequences.text: The proposed identities P_R = 2*P_L and P_R = kappa^2/(4*pi*G) jointly imply P_L = kappa^2/(8*pi*G). Thus the two pressure coordinates remain distinct on this Schwarzschild family.
consequences.title: Conditional normal-scale pressure formula

consequences.text: With the adopted coordinate-work definitions, the proposed radial force and volume-work identities express the common radius coefficient of F_L*dL, F_R*dR, M*kappa*dR, and P_R*dV. They do not identify this positive work with dU.
consequences.title: Scalar content of the retained positive work chain

consequences.text: The proposed thermal and work-product identities make both products equal to U. Together with the adopted mass normalization, the candidate sum has two equal contributions, each M*c^2/2. The physical decomposition interpretation is not established by these scalar equalities.
consequences.title: Equal products in the algebraic mass-energy sum

consequences.text: The adopted normalization makes M*c^2 = 2*U throughout the radius family. Accordingly, the proposed first-law coefficient T*dS/dR = c^4/(2*G) is twice dU/dR = c^4/(4*G), rather than an assertion that dU = T*dS along this family.
consequences.title: Mass first law differs from the derivative of the boundary potential

consequences.text: If the proposed candidates are established, the adopted spherical equilibrium-screen assignments give a matching potential and energy expression, a screen-density pressure relation, and the radius coefficient of the printed first law. Their physical prescriptions remain premises.
consequences.title: Conditional screen thermodynamics

consequences.text: If established, the radial-pressure candidate identifies the source's unit length-radius conversion with P = P_L, while the pressure candidates express the same screen scale using surface gravity or inverse radius. No Schwarzschild factor of two is used.
consequences.title: FRW work-coordinate normalization

consequences.text: The proposed flat and curved substitutions and the density rewrites test conditional scalar consistency. Even if established, they do not assert an acceleration law, set a conservation expression to zero, or prove equivalence to Einstein–FRW dynamics.
consequences.title: Cosmological expressions without a dynamical derivation

consequences.text: The derivative and coefficient candidates isolate the proposed δκ-to-δL transformation and its comparison with −F_L. Their scope is conditional on the cited canonical starting response and the adopted mechanical model.
consequences.title: Scalar content of the retained canonical chain

consequences.text: The potential and force-ratio candidates concern differentiation of the adopted boundary potential. The canonical coefficient comparison uses a separately disclosed cited response rather than defining that response from the desired force identification.
consequences.title: Separate mechanical and canonical premises

compiledSubjectExplanations.title: Gravitational boundary mechanics and horizon thermodynamics

paragraphs.text:
The construction starts with a fixed clock normalization, positive surface gravity κ, horizon area A, and acceleration length L = c²/κ. It adopts the boundary potential U = Aκc²/(8πG), attributed in the source to a specified Einstein boundary prescription. Substitution gives U = c⁴A/(8πGL), which the checker confirms algebraically. This separates two questions: the substitution is checked, while the gravitational justification of the adopted potential remains a cited physical input. The general scalar model treats A and L as independent positive coordinates, with the physical constants fixed.

This is a conditional mathematical consequence of the cited inputs; physical applicability, explanatory prose, and novelty still require independent assessment.
