conditions: Adopted input — Clock, positive surface gravity, and acceleration length (version source-0dab6492b681): Use a specified clock, positive surface gravity κ, horizon area A, and acceleration length L = c²/κ.
Adopted input — Prescribed Einstein boundary potential (version source-0dab6492b681): Adopt U(A,L) = Aκc²/(8πG) under the specified Einstein boundary prescription.
Adopted input — Independent-coordinate mechanical model (version source-0dab6492b681): For the general response calculation, treat A and L as independent scalar coordinates and hold c and G fixed.

Adopted input — Mechanical response conventions (version source-0dab6492b681): Use the mass equivalent U/c², the positive area derivative for Π, the negative fixed-area length derivative for F_L, and force per area for P_L.

Adopted input — Work-coordinate convention (version source-0dab6492b681): Surface stress pairs with area change, force pairs with horizon-scale change, and work coefficients must transform with a change of work coordinate.
Adopted input — Hawking–Unruh temperature (version source-0dab6492b681): Adopt T = ℏc/(2πk_B L).
Adopted input — Einstein area entropy and Planck-area convention (version source-0dab6492b681): Adopt the printed Einstein area entropy with coefficient k_B/(4ℓ_P²), using ℓ_P² = ℏG/c³.

Adopted input — Rindler geometric normalization (version source-0dab6492b681): For Rindler, use the acceleration length c²/a_obs as the normal horizon distance on the instantaneous rest slice, with independent planar patch area A.
Adopted input — Schwarzschild stationary family (version source-0dab6492b681): For Schwarzschild, constrain the area to 4πR² and the acceleration length to 2R, with time normalized at infinity.
Adopted input — Schwarzschild mass normalization (version source-0dab6492b681): Use the printed Schwarzschild identification U = Mc²/2, keeping M distinct from M_U.

Adopted input — Schwarzschild areal volume and radial work (version source-0dab6492b681): Use areal volume 4πR³/3 and define radial work coefficients by the printed equality of F_L dL, F_R dR, and P_R dV.

Adopted input — Instantaneous-equilibrium FRW screen (version source-0dab6492b681): For the FRW application, adopt a separate instantaneous-equilibrium screen assignment with L = R_A and spherical areal volume 4πR_A³/3.
Adopted input — FRW spherical area translation (version source-0dab6492b681): For scalar translation of the FRW screen formulas, use A = 4πR_A².
Adopted input — Einstein–Misner–Sharp identification (version source-0dab6492b681): Adopt the identification of U with E and the printed energy E = c⁴R_A/(2G).
Adopted input — Density convention (version source-0dab6492b681): Interpret ρ as energy per areal volume, as required by the printed relation E = ρV.
Adopted input — Flat-FRW apparent radius (version source-0dab6492b681): In the flat-FRW application, adopt R_A = c/H.
Adopted input — Expansion law in screen-pressure variables (version source-0dab6492b681): Adopt H² = (8πG/c²)P as the stated flat-FRW expansion law.
Adopted input — Acceleration law in screen-pressure variables (version source-0dab6492b681): Adopt 2ä/(ac²) = −κ_E(P + p_m) as the stated acceleration law.
Adopted input — Conservation law in screen-pressure variables (version source-0dab6492b681): Adopt Ṗ + H(3P + p_m) = 0 as the stated conservation law.

Adopted input — Cosmological notation and matter scope (version source-0dab6492b681): Use the printed Hubble-rate and κ_E conventions; p_m denotes total bulk pressure, is distinct from screen pressure P, and includes vacuum contributions consistently.
Adopted input — Curved-FRW apparent radius (version source-0dab6492b681): Adopt R_A = c/√(H² + kc²/a²) for curved FRW.

Adopted input — Selected canonical sector (version source-0dab6492b681): Restrict the quoted canonical response to a fixed clock, fixed cuts, the stated mixed boundary prescription, vanishing null expansion, and vanishing variation of that expansion.
Adopted input — Canonical scalar response (version source-0dab6492b681): Adopt the quoted response Θ_κ^(0)/Δτ = [Ac²/(8πG)] δκ.

Adopted input — Scalar domains and constant conventions (version source-0dab6492b681): For candidate scalar checks, take the displayed physical constants as fixed and nonzero, restrict denominators to nonzero values, use positive areas and radii, and require a positive curved-FRW radicand. The printed flat positive-radius assignment selects H > 0 when c > 0.

Adopted input — Ordinary derivative-coefficient translation (version source-0dab6492b681): Read the scalar d and δ relations through ordinary derivative coefficients with sufficient differentiability. Differentiate the general potential before applying stationary-family constraints; use total family derivatives afterward.
Assumption: Model 1: The clock normalization is fixed throughout. This is a source premise, not an algebraic conclusion.

Assumption: Model 1: A and L are independent scalar coordinates for the general response calculation. A derivative with respect to one holds the other fixed; no stationary-radius constraint is imposed.
Assumption: Model 1: c and G are fixed positive physical constants. pi is the fixed positive dimensionless circle constant, with no rational approximation.
Assumption: Model 1: The scalar model uses A > 0 and L > 0, excluding degenerate areas and lengths. These explicit domain restrictions supplement the source's stated positive surface gravity.
Assumption: Model 1: The source relation L = c²/κ is encoded equivalently as κ = c²/L so that L remains an independent differentiation coordinate.

Assumption: Model 1: The Einstein boundary potential is adopted in its source form U = Aκc²/(8πG). Its gravitational origin and the boundary prescription attributed to reference [1] are not derived here.

Assumption: Model 1: The mass equivalent and response conventions are adopted through the definitions of M_U, Pi, F_L and P_L below. The minus sign in F_L distinguishes the negative length contribution to dU from positive work F_L dL.

Assumption: Model 1: Scalar d-relations are translated into ordinary partial-derivative coefficient equalities on the positive independent-(A,L) domain. This translation does not assert a general covariant or field-space differential-form theorem.
Assumption: Model 1: The Rindler distance interpretation and independence of planar patch area are retained as geometric premises, not inferred from the potential.
Assumption: Model 2: This batch uses independent scalar coordinates A and L, both positive, with the specified clock held fixed. No stationary-radius or cosmological family constraint is imposed.
Assumption: Model 2: The constants c, G, hbar and kB are fixed and positive; pi is the fixed positive circle constant. These conventional domain restrictions make all displayed denominators nonzero.
Assumption: Model 2: The acceleration-length prescription is encoded as kappa = c^2/L. Thus kappa varies with L and is not held fixed when differentiating with respect to L.

Assumption: Model 2: The source's prescribed Einstein boundary potential is an adopted physical input. Its gravitational justification and the cited boundary prescription are not established by this package.

Assumption: Model 2: The mechanical conventions are Pi = partial U/partial A at fixed L, F_L = -partial U/partial L at fixed A, and P_L = F_L/A. The negative length contribution to dU is distinct from the positive work coefficient F_L.
Assumption: Model 2: The Hawking–Unruh temperature, Einstein area entropy and Planck-area convention are separately adopted inputs, not consequences of the mechanical potential.
Assumption: Model 2: Scalar differential notation is translated into ordinary partial-derivative coefficients with the other independent coordinate and all physical constants held fixed.
Assumption: Model 2: The product A L is not identified with an areal volume.
Assumption: Model 2: The source's thermal-independence statements are retained as scope statements about the mechanical construction, not as proofs of physical applicability.

Assumption: Model 3: Adopt A = 4*pi*R^2, L = 2*R, and areal volume V = 4*pi*R^3/3 as the source-stated family assignments.
Assumption: Model 3: Adopt the acceleration-length relation L = c^2/kappa, encoded equivalently as kappa = c^2/L on the positive domain.
Assumption: Model 3: Adopt the prescribed Einstein boundary potential U = A*kappa*c^2/(8*pi*G). Its gravitational justification is an input, not a consequence of the candidate identities.
Assumption: Model 3: Adopt the Schwarzschild normalization U = M*c^2/2 and solve it for M before taking total radius derivatives. M is not the mass equivalent U/c^2.

Assumption: Model 3: Take c, G, hbar, kB, and pi as fixed positive constants. pi denotes the usual dimensionless circle constant, without a rational approximation. Positivity of constants and geometric coordinates is an explicit domain convention.
Assumption: Model 3: A_free and L_free are independent positive auxiliary coordinates used only for the fixed-area length derivative. They are not additional Schwarzschild family coordinates.

Assumption: Model 3: Compute the negative fixed-area length derivative of the prescribed potential before substituting A_free = A and L_free = L. This preserves the distinction between a mechanical response and a total radius derivative.
Assumption: Model 3: Adopt P_L = F_L/A. Define F_R and P_R through the source's positive work-coordinate transformation, rather than assuming their proposed factors or pressure formulas.
Assumption: Model 3: Adopt the Hawking–Unruh temperature, Einstein area entropy, and Planck-area convention exactly as encoded in the symbol definitions.

Assumption: Model 3: Interpret scalar differential relations through ordinary derivative coefficients with sufficient differentiability. Only R varies along the stationary family; all physical constants remain fixed.
Assumption: Model 3: The positive work chain F_L*dL = F_R*dR = P_R*dV is not the complete differential of U. In the independent-coordinate model the length contribution to dU has the opposite sign.
Assumption: Model 3: Positive domains assigned to derived quantities follow from these adopted positive inputs and the displayed derivative definitions; they do not impose any target equality.
Assumption: Model 4: The clock normalization is fixed. The physical constants c, G, hbar and kB are fixed and positive; pi is the fixed positive dimensionless circle constant.
Assumption: Model 4: R_A is an independent positive radius. Differentiation is along this nondegenerate, sufficiently differentiable screen family, with all physical constants fixed.
Assumption: Model 4: This is the source's separate instantaneous-equilibrium FRW assignment, not a stationary worldtube or the Schwarzschild family.
Assumption: Model 4: Adopt L = R_A and V = 4*pi*R_A^3/3. Also adopt A = 4*pi*R_A^2 as the explicitly disclosed inferred spherical-area premise; this area relation is not expressly printed for FRW.

Assumption: Model 4: Independently adopt the cited energy formula E = c^4*R_A/(2*G). U = E is not imposed as a definition; their independently specified expressions are compared.
Assumption: Model 4: Define rho = E/V and interpret rho as energy density, not mass density. This dimensional interpretation is an inferred premise.

Assumption: Model 4: Adopt the Hawking–Unruh temperature, Einstein area entropy, and Planck-area convention. The Planck area hbar*G/c^3 is expanded inside the entropy definition rather than represented by a square-root symbol.

Assumption: Model 4: For the conservation-expression rewrite only, v_R is an arbitrary instantaneous radial rate. Represent a time derivative of a radius-dependent scalar f as v_R*diff(f,R_A); no evolution equation for R_A is assumed.

Assumption: Model 4: H is restricted to the positive expanding branch. The flat calculation uses the explicit family substitution H = c/R_A, equivalent on this domain to the supplied R_A = c/H; the expansion law is not assumed to prove itself.
Assumption: Model 4: For the curved calculation, choose a length-dimensional positive scale factor a and dimensionless real curvature parameter k. No discrete normalization of k is asserted.

Assumption: Model 4: The curved-radius input is used only through its squared relation. The explicit substitution k = (a^2/c^2)*(c^2/R_A^2 - H^2) is an adopted rational parametrization of that relation, not an independent derivation of it. Its radicand equals the positive c^2/R_A^2.

Assumption: Model 4: Adopt kappa_E = 8*pi*G/c^4. The independent real symbol p_m denotes total bulk pressure, distinct in meaning from screen pressure; no bulk equation of state or allocation of vacuum contributions is supplied.
Assumption: Model 5: The clock normalization is fixed throughout. The constants c and G are fixed and positive; pi is the fixed positive mathematical constant π, not a rational approximation.

Assumption: Model 5: A and L are independent positive scalar coordinates in the general mechanical model. Differentiation with respect to L holds A and all constants fixed; no stationary-family constraint is imposed.

Assumption: Model 5: The printed normalization L = c²/κ is adopted through its equivalent positive-coordinate expression κ(L) = c²/L. Positivity of A and L is an explicit model restriction; positive κ is stated by the source.
Assumption: Model 5: The prescribed Einstein boundary potential U = Aκc²/(8πG) is adopted as a physical input attributed to reference [1], not derived from the scalar calculations.
Assumption: Model 5: The source's mechanical sign convention is adopted: F_L is minus the fixed-area partial derivative of U with respect to L.
Assumption: Model 5: The quoted canonical response [Ac²/(8πG)] δκ is adopted only under the source's fixed clock, fixed cuts, stated mixed boundary prescription, θ = 0, and δθ = 0 restrictions.
Assumption: Model 5: C_kappa denotes only the scalar coefficient Ac²/(8πG) in that cited response. It does not independently define or establish Θ_κ^(0), Δτ, or the canonical boundary one-form.

paragraphs.text:
The checked consequences are Π = U/A and F_L = U/L. With the adopted mass equivalent M_U = U/c², this also gives F_L = M_Uκ. That resemblance to mass times acceleration is a scalar identity within this model, not an independently established force law. Defining force density by P_L = F_L/A gives P_L = Π/L = κ²/(8πG). The products U = ΠA = F_LL = P_LAL are all checked representations of the same potential; they do not identify separate energy stores, and AL is not automatically a spherical volume. Finally, Π has no area dependence at fixed L, and A(∂Π/∂L) = −F_L. Together these checked coefficients give A dΠ = −F_L dL in the independent-coordinate model.

parentDecision.parentScope: Energy, mass, conservation laws, mechanical work, entropy, and temperature in gravitational systems, including bulk and boundary formulations, black holes, and cosmological spacetimes.

sections.text:
The starting point is a specified clock normalization, positive surface gravity \(\kappa\), horizon area \(A\), and acceleration length \(L=c^2/\kappa\). Under the adopted Einstein boundary prescription,
\[U=\frac{A\kappa c^2}{8\pi G}=\frac{c^4A}{8\pi GL}.\]
Thus the prescribed energy grows with area at fixed acceleration length and decreases with acceleration length at fixed area.

For the general mechanical calculation, \(A\) and \(L\) are independent positive scalar coordinates, with physical constants and the clock normalization held fixed. Rewriting \(\kappa=c^2/L\) is an algebraic coordinate change; it does not establish the gravitational origin of the potential. Radius constraints enter only when a particular geometric family is selected.
sections.title: The boundary potential and its chosen coordinates

sections.text:
The two independent derivatives define different mechanical responses:
\[\Pi=\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial A}\right)_L=\frac{c^4}{8\pi GL},\qquad F_L=-\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial L}\right)_A=\frac{Ac^4}{8\pi GL^2}.\]
Here \(\Pi\) is the coefficient paired with area change, while \(F_L\) is the positive work coefficient paired with acceleration-length change. Their signs give
\[dU=\Pi\,dA-F_L\,dL.\]
Increasing area raises the potential; increasing length at fixed area lowers it. The positive work expression \(F_LdL\) is therefore not itself the length contribution to \(dU\).

These derivatives must be evaluated before imposing a relation between area and radius. A total derivative along a constrained family includes both area and length changes and is not interchangeable with either partial derivative.
sections.title: Area stress and length force

sections.text:
Defining the mass equivalent \(M_U=U/c^2\) and force per area \(P_L=F_L/A\) gives
\[\Pi=\frac{U}{A},\qquad F_L=\frac{U}{L}=M_U\kappa,\qquad P_L=\frac{\Pi}{L}=\frac{\kappa^2}{8\pi G}.\]
The resemblance of \(F_L=M_U\kappa\) to mass times acceleration is a scalar identity within this prescription, not an independently established force law.

The products \(U=\Pi A=F_LL=P_LAL\) are representations of the same potential, not separate energy stores. In particular, \(AL\) is not automatically a spherical volume. Because \(\Pi\) depends on \(L\) but not on \(A\), its variation also satisfies \(A\,d\Pi=-F_L\,dL\) in the independent-coordinate model.
sections.title: Equivalent mechanical expressions

sections.text:
Temperature and entropy are separately adopted through
\[T=\frac{\hbar c}{2\pi k_BL},\qquad S=\frac{k_BA}{4\ell_P^2},\qquad \ell_P^2=\frac{\hbar G}{c^3}.\]
With these prescriptions, their product agrees with the boundary potential: \(TS=U\). This checks compatibility of the chosen expressions; it does not derive Hawking–Unruh temperature or area entropy from the mechanical potential.

Entropy depends only on area, and the checked area coefficient gives \(\Pi\,dA=T\,dS\). This translates the area response into thermal language. It must be distinguished from the product identity \(U=TS\): multiplying \(T\) by \(dS\) is not the same operation as differentiating \(TS\).
sections.title: Thermal meaning requires additional inputs

sections.text:
A separate canonical input quotes the response \(\Theta_\kappa^{(0)}/\Delta\tau=[Ac^2/(8\pi G)]\,\delta\kappa\). Its scope is restricted to fixed clock and cuts, the stated mixed boundary prescription, and vanishing null expansion and variation of that expansion.

Under the ordinary scalar translation \(\delta\kappa=(d\kappa/dL)\delta L\),
\[\frac{d\kappa}{dL}=-\frac{c^2}{L^2},\qquad \frac{Ac^2}{8\pi G}\frac{d\kappa}{dL}=-\frac{Ac^4}{8\pi GL^2}=-F_L.\]
The transformed coefficient therefore matches the negative length-response coefficient. This is a conditional coefficient comparison within the selected sector, not a derivation of the canonical boundary object or an unrestricted field-space identity.
sections.title: A restricted canonical comparison

sections.text:
The Schwarzschild stationary family uses time normalized at infinity, \(A=4\pi R^2\), \(L=2R\), and areal volume \(V=4\pi R^3/3\). These are family assignments, unlike the independent coordinates used to define \(F_L\). The adopted mass normalization is \(U=Mc^2/2\), so \(M\) must remain distinct from \(M_U=U/c^2\).

The same positive work is expressed in different coordinates by
\[F_L\,dL=F_R\,dR=P_R\,dV.\]
Because a radius change produces twice that change in \(L\), the checked coefficients are
\[F_R=2F_L=M\kappa,\qquad P_R=2P_L=\frac{\kappa^2}{4\pi G}.\]
Equivalently, \(P_R(dV/dR)=M\kappa\). The factor of two comes from changing the work coordinate, not from introducing another interaction. Fractional changes nevertheless agree: \(dL/L=dR/R\), or \((1/L)(dL/dR)=1/R\).
sections.title: Schwarzschild: changing the work coordinate

sections.text:
On this stationary family, the checked product relations are \(TS=U\), \(F_LL=U\), and \(U=3P_RV\). Together with the adopted mass normalization, they give
\[Mc^2=TS+F_LL.\]
This is an algebraic relation among products; it should not be read as evidence that the boundary potential contains two independently established energy reservoirs.

A distinct check concerns total derivatives along the radius family:
\[d(Mc^2)=T\,dS,\qquad c^2\frac{dM}{dR}=T\frac{dS}{dR}.\]
These statements concern the Schwarzschild mass energy, not the independent-coordinate differential of \(U\). Keeping the mass normalization, work-coordinate transformation and type of derivative explicit prevents apparently similar formulas from being conflated.
sections.title: Schwarzschild: products versus family variations

sections.text:
The cosmological application is an instantaneous-equilibrium screen assignment, not the Schwarzschild stationary family or a stationary worldtube. It sets \(L=R_A\) and \(V=4\pi R_A^3/3\). The scalar translation also makes explicit an inferred spherical-area premise, \(A=4\pi R_A^2\), and interprets \(\rho=E/V\) as energy density.

With those inputs, the boundary potential agrees with the independently prescribed energy \(E=c^4R_A/(2G)\). Equality of the expressions is checked; the physical Einstein–Misner–Sharp identification remains an adopted input. Here \(dL/dR_A=1\), so the work-coordinate transformation gives \(P=P_L\), without the Schwarzschild factor of two.

The checked screen relations are \(P=\rho/3\) and the radius coefficient of
\[dE=T\,dS-P\,dV.\]
The pressure \(P\) describes screen work. Its relation to energy density is not a bulk-matter equation of state.
sections.title: FRW: a separate equilibrium-screen prescription

sections.text:
Writing \(\kappa_E=8\pi G/c^4\), the equilibrium-screen pressure satisfies \(1/R_A^2=\kappa_EP\). For flat FRW, the adopted apparent radius \(R_A=c/H\), on the positive expanding branch, translates this into
\[H^2=\frac{8\pi G}{c^2}P.\]
Here \(H\) is the Hubble expansion rate. The checked statement is conditional on the radius and screen assignments, rather than an independent derivation of cosmological dynamics from the boundary potential.

For curved FRW, the separate radius prescription gives \(R_A^2(H^2+kc^2/a^2)=c^2\), where \(a\) is the scale factor and \(k\) the curvature parameter. Combining it with the screen-pressure relation yields
\[H^2+\frac{kc^2}{a^2}=\frac{8\pi G}{c^2}P.\]
The curved scalar check uses the supplied squared-radius relation under a rational parametrization with positive radicand; it does not establish that geometric prescription.
sections.title: Apparent radius and expansion expressions

sections.text:
The screen pressure \(P\) remains distinct from total bulk pressure \(p_m\). Substitution of \(\rho=3P\) checks the acceleration-coefficient equality
\[-\frac{\kappa_E}{3}(\rho+3p_m)=-\kappa_E(P+p_m).\]
This supports expressing the adopted acceleration law as \(2\ddot a/(ac^2)=-\kappa_E(P+p_m)\); it does not supply a bulk equation of state.

For differentiable screen assignments, the chain rule also checks
\[\frac{\dot\rho+3H(\rho+p_m)}{3}=\dot P+H(3P+p_m).\]
Consequently, an adopted conservation law can be written as \(\dot P+H(3P+p_m)=0\). The checked rewrite permits an arbitrary instantaneous radial rate and supplies no independent evolution equation for \(R_A\). Equilibrium screen identities and cosmological evolution laws therefore remain different levels of input.
sections.title: Rewriting adopted dynamical laws

sections.text:
The common mechanism is scalar differentiation of an adopted boundary potential, followed by carefully specified thermal and work-coordinate translations. Its applications depend on keeping independent-coordinate mechanics, the infinity-normalized Schwarzschild family, the restricted canonical sector and the separate instantaneous-equilibrium FRW assignment distinct.

The mathematical checks do not validate the gravitational boundary prescription, thermal inputs, geometric energy identification, physical applicability or source fidelity. They also do not establish unrestricted covariant variation identities, nonequilibrium screen dynamics or a bulk-matter equation of state. Those extensions require justification beyond the supplied coefficient comparisons.

The contributions remain provisional because originality and originating-source chronology are unresolved, not because the reported conditional algebra has failed. No result here is certified as a first discovery.

sections.text:
Inputs. The manuscript fixes a clock, takes positive surface gravity \(\kappa\), introduces \(L=c^2/\kappa\), and adopts the boundary potential \(U=A\kappa c^2/(8\pi G)=Ac^4/(8\pi GL)\). Its general scalar calculation treats \(A\) and \(L\) as independent coordinates. The gravitational prescription underlying this potential is an input, not something derived by differentiating it.

Construction. With constants fixed, the prescribed derivative conventions give
\[
\Pi=\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial A}\right)_L=\frac{c^4}{8\pi GL},\qquad
F_L=-\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial L}\right)_A=\frac{Ac^4}{8\pi GL^2}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
dU=\Pi\,dA-F_L\,dL,\qquad
F_L=\frac{U}{L}=M_U\kappa,\qquad
P_L=\frac{F_L}{A}=\frac{\kappa^2}{8\pi G},
\]
where \(M_U=U/c^2\). These are derivative-defined generalized responses. Calling them a force and pressure adds a physical interpretation to their algebraic construction.

Additional inputs and outputs. Adopting Hawking–Unruh temperature and Einstein area entropy produces \(U=TS\) and \(\Pi\,dA=T\,dS\). Imposing the Schwarzschild family only after differentiation yields radial work coefficients and \(P_R=2P_L\). A separate instantaneous-equilibrium FRW assignment, \(L=R_A\), together with spherical area, areal volume, and the Einstein–Misner–Sharp energy identification, yields \(U=E\), \(P=P_L=\rho/3\), and the displayed radius-family first-law relation. Finally, an adopted canonical scalar response proportional to \(A\,\delta\kappa\) is rewritten as \(-F_L\delta L\) under restricted boundary conditions.

Mathematical evidence. The actual supplied report has status “checked.” For example, b1-g01_area_coefficient, b1-g01_length_coefficient, b1-g01_mass_acceleration_identity, and b1-g01_pressure_surface_gravity each report zero residual and consistent dimensions under their declared domains. This supports the stated scalar implications of the adopted potential; it does not independently establish that potential, a physical boundary force, or a new interaction.
sections.title: Inputs → construction → claimed outputs

sections.text:
The simplest interpretation is that the adopted boundary energy increases with area but decreases with acceleration length. The area response \(\Pi\) therefore multiplies an area change, while the positive coefficient \(F_L\) enters the energy differential with a minus sign. The force-like formula \(F_L=M_U\kappa\) follows because both the mass equivalent and acceleration are defined from the same potential and length scale; it is not an independent test of a gravitational force law.

The two mechanical coefficients also reorganize the thermal differential. With the stipulated \(T\propto L^{-1}\) and \(S\propto A\), one has \(dU=T\,dS+S\,dT\), where the second term becomes \(-F_L\,dL\). Thus the length-work description is a mechanical reparameterization of the temperature-variation contribution when thermal inputs are used. The report checks \(U=TS\) and the area coefficient through b2-g02_thermal_product and b2-g02_thermal_area. Thermal input is nevertheless unnecessary for obtaining the derivative-defined \(F_L\) and \(P_L\).

Rindler supplies the motivating distance interpretation: \(c^2/a_{\rm obs}\) is the normal horizon distance on the stated rest slice, independently of planar patch area. That does not make \(L\) a universal proper distance in every spacetime.

For Schwarzschild, \(L=2R\), so preserving work requires \(F_R=2F_L=M\kappa\), and \(P_R=F_R/(4\pi R^2)=2P_L\). Here \(M_U=M/2\), not \(M\). The reported checks b3-schw_radial_force_factor, b3-schw_pressure_factor, and b3-schw_mass_first_law support these family-specific scalar relations. The expression \(Mc^2=TS+F_LL\) contains two equal products, each equal to \(U\); it does not by itself establish two independently measurable energy reservoirs or change the retained mass first law.

For the FRW screen, \(L=R_A\) instead gives \(P=P_L\). The resulting \(P=\rho/3\) is a relation between screen pressure and energy density, not a radiation equation of state for the separately named bulk pressure \(p_m\). Also, \(AL\) is not the areal volume: on this spherical screen \(AL=3V\). The screen first law is checked only as a radius coefficient by b4-frw_first_law_radius.
sections.title: A faithful physical reading

sections.text:
The closest displayed antecedent is the selected full text of The Structure of the Gravitational Action and its relation with Horizon Thermodynamics and Emergent Gravity Paradigm. Its passages excerpt-18, excerpt-275, and excerpt-422 identify horizon surface heat content with \(TS\) and separate suitable boundary variations into \(T\delta S\) and \(S\delta T\). The displayed near-horizon calculation contains an area-weighted surface-gravity variation in the paper’s conventions. This is substantial prior structure behind the manuscript’s potential and canonical/thermal translation, although restoring the manuscript’s units, clock, and variation conventions requires an explicit map.

Gravity Degrees of Freedom on a Null Surface supplies a second direct foundation. Selected passages excerpt-175, excerpt-181, excerpt-198, and excerpt-219 display surface-gravity variations, boundary and corner actions, and a scalar momentum combining surface gravity with expansion. The same excerpts explain how total variations redistribute terms between canonical and action contributions. Thus area/surface-gravity boundary mechanics and its dependence on polarization are not established here for the first time.

General gravitational charges on null hypersurfaces makes that qualification especially important. Its displayed potentials in excerpt-194 contain different coefficients of \(\delta k\) and different area-form contributions. Other supplied passages discuss boundary restrictions, covariance, and corner ambiguities. These selected derivations confirm that a response cannot be characterized solely by extracting an \(A\delta\kappa\) term without specifying its surrounding potential and admissible variations. The prior paper’s \(k\), and the null-vector notation in the other paper, must not be identified with the manuscript’s symbols without a convention map.

The retrieved Wieland, Reisenberger, and Sheikh-Jabbari records identify relevant null-boundary or null-data topics, but their supplied evidence is metadata only. In particular, Wieland’s relevance description mentions abstract-level content, yet no abstract is actually supplied; it cannot support a detailed theorem comparison here. The manuscript’s cosmological references are listed in its bibliography, but corresponding retrieved paper records or passages are absent, so their detailed FRW results cannot be independently assessed from this payload.
sections.title: Established foundations and concrete overlap

sections.text:
The precise candidate advance is not the existence of horizon heat content \(TS\), an area/surface-gravity canonical structure, or the temperature-variation term. Those have concrete antecedents in the selected primary passages. Rather, the manuscript proposes selecting the geometrically motivated coordinate \(L=c^2/\kappa\), identifying its positive generalized work coefficient \(F_L\), and consistently distinguishing its force density \(P_L\) from coefficients conjugate to radius or areal volume.

This could be a useful refinement if the author demonstrates that the selected boundary prescription makes the length response physically meaningful, rather than merely a convenient coordinate rewrite. The Schwarzschild/FRW contrast is particularly clear: \(dL/dR=2\) in one assignment and \(dL/dR_A=1\) in the other, explaining the different pressure factors without treating either coefficient as coordinate-independent.

The canonical assertion is conditional. The report checks b5-g05_canonical_length_coeff and b5-g05_canonical_force_coeff: the adopted coefficient \(Ac^2/(8\pi G)\), multiplied by \(d\kappa/dL\), equals \(-F_L\). It does not reconstruct the gravitational one-form. Relative to the displayed Hopfmüller–Freidel and Odak passages, the missing substantive step is a documented reduction from a specified full potential, with its area, vector, shear, and corner contributions, to the manuscript’s selected scalar response. Merely imposing \(\theta=\delta\theta=0\) does not visibly remove every other contribution in the supplied prior formulas.

The selected excerpts do not establish whether the exact acceleration-length interpretation or this cross-regime presentation appeared elsewhere in those complete papers. The unavailable discovery searches and narrow metadata results cannot resolve that priority question. Any claim of difference should therefore be limited to a proposed formulation whose distinct explanatory value still needs demonstration.
sections.title: What might differ from the supplied prior work

sections.text:
The established background supplied here connects gravitational boundary actions, horizon heat content, and canonical variations. Within that setting, the manuscript could contribute an economical mechanical vocabulary: area controls a surface response, acceleration length controls a force-like response, and work coefficients transform when one changes the horizon-size coordinate. Its potentially useful contribution is therefore organizational and interpretive, connecting existing boundary thermodynamics to geometrically normalized work variables without proposing a new interaction.

The cosmological application is best presented as a conditional change of variables. Using \(P=\rho/3\), the manuscript writes the flat Einstein–FRW equations as
\[
H^2=\frac{8\pi G}{c^2}P,\qquad
\frac{2\ddot a}{ac^2}=-\kappa_E(P+p_m),\qquad
\dot P+H(3P+p_m)=0,
\]
with \(\kappa_E=8\pi G/c^4\). The curved-screen relation is \(R_A^{-2}=\kappa_E P\). This may clarify how a chosen horizon-scale coefficient tracks cosmological energy density, but it does not explain cosmological dynamics independently of the Einstein–Misner–Sharp identification and adopted gravitational equations.

The report’s b4-frw_flat_pressure_rewrite and b4-frw_inverse_radius_pressure support the corresponding conditional scalar substitutions. Its b4-frw_acceleration_coefficient_rewrite and b4-frw_conservation_expression_rewrite check density substitutions and a chain-rule expression, not the acceleration or conservation laws themselves. Consequently, the manuscript has not supplied a new dynamical mechanism, a matter equation of state, or an observational prediction. Its broader explanatory value would depend on showing what the length-work organization clarifies that the already established \(T\delta S+S\delta T\) and polarization-based descriptions do not.
sections.title: Potential contribution to the wider explanation

sections.text:
Boundary prescription and admissible variations. The supplied page does not specify enough of the mixed boundary action, corner treatment, normalization, or allowed field variations to reconstruct its canonical claim. The selected primary passages show why these choices matter. A revision should identify the exact starting potential, restore units, map null-normal conventions to the specified clock, and exhibit the reduction to the stated scalar sector. It should also demonstrate that varying \(\kappa\) remains admissible under its boundary conditions. A nonzero selected action response should not be conflated with a complete variational principle or a unique boundary Hamiltonian.

Coordinate and regime limits. Independent-coordinate derivatives must precede Schwarzschild or FRW family substitutions; total family derivatives are different operations. The report preserves this distinction, but the compact manuscript should make it explicit. Fixed clock normalization is indispensable: \(L\), \(U\), and the response coefficients depend on that choice. The Rindler distance interpretation does not establish an invariant normal distance for all horizons. The claimed stationary de Sitter realization is named but not worked through on the supplied page. Evolving FRW is explicitly a separate instantaneous-equilibrium assignment, not a consequence of the stationary-null calculation. Its temperature choice, applicability away from equilibrium, treatment of vacuum contributions, and connection between screen work and bulk pressure need physical justification. The cited cosmology papers are not available here for the necessary comparison of energy, temperature, work, and sign conventions.

Scope of the actual checks. The supplied formal-lab-sympy-v2 report, using SymPy 1.14.0, is linked to package digest 218eb4ef06287c6920a1962a4c70f6133c27e188477b32dc47c18f3d62b0d2ef. Every listed claim has status “checked,” with zero residual and consistent dimensions; no contradicted or inconclusive status is listed. These results apply only to the declared scalar models and domains. Notably, b3-potential_length_substitution is explicitly classified as a definition-restatement. The curved-radius check b4-frw_curved_squared_radius uses an adopted rational parametrization of the squared radius relation; it is not an independent derivation of that geometry or its square-root branch. None of the checks establishes general field-space identities, physical uniqueness, novelty, or empirical validity.

Source and search limits. Only one manuscript page is supplied; its referenced companion manuscripts are unavailable. All three arXiv discovery requests were unavailable and must not be counted as successful searches. report.summary: The manuscript offers a compact acceleration-length representation of an adopted Einstein horizon-boundary potential. Its force, pressure, thermal products, and family-specific work conversions are supported as conditional scalar identities by the supplied mathematical report. The strongest possible contribution is an interpretive connection between established boundary responses and a geometrically normalized work coordinate—not a new interaction or independently derived cosmological dynamics. Selected primary passages establish substantial overlap with earlier surface-Hamiltonian, null-canonical, and membrane-pressure constructions. Whether the proposed interpretation provides additional physical content or a distinct conceptual advance remains unresolved.

sections.text:
Inputs. The construction fixes a clock normalization, takes positive surface gravity \(\kappa\), and introduces \(L=c^2/\kappa\). Its essential gravitational input is the prescribed potential
\[
U(A,L)=\frac{A\kappa c^2}{8\pi G}=\frac{c^4A}{8\pi GL}.
\]
The general response calculation treats \(A\) and \(L\) as independent coordinates, with physical constants fixed. The potential and its gravitational interpretation are premises; they are not derived from the subsequent differentiation.

Construction. Define the area response, negative length derivative, and force density by
\[
\Pi=\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial A}\right)_L,\qquad F_L=-\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial L}\right)_A,\qquad P_L=\frac{F_L}{A}.
\]
These give
\[
dU=\Pi\,dA-F_L\,dL,\qquad \Pi=\frac{U}{A},\qquad F_L=\frac{U}{L}=M_U\kappa,\qquad P_L=\frac{\kappa^2}{8\pi G},
\]
where \(M_U=U/c^2\). Thus the advertised mass–acceleration relation follows from the adopted potential and coordinate map; it is not an additional dynamical law.

Additional inputs and outputs. Independently adopting Hawking–Unruh temperature and Einstein area entropy yields \(U=TS\) and \(\Pi\,dA=T\,dS\). Schwarzschild geometry supplies \(A=4\pi R^2\), \(L=2R\), and \(U=Mc^2/2\), leading to the stated radial-work conversion. The cosmological application separately assigns \(L=R_A\), spherical area and volume, and Einstein–Misner–Sharp energy, leading to \(U=E\), \(P=\rho/3\), and the radius-family identity \(dE=T\,dS-P\,dV\). Here \(\rho\) is energy density, not mass density.

The canonical connection is another conditional input: under fixed clock, fixed cuts, the chosen boundary prescription, and \(\theta=\delta\theta=0\), the manuscript adopts a response proportional to \(A\,\delta\kappa\). Changing coordinates then gives \(-F_L\delta L\). Stationary horizons and evolving FRW screens are explicitly different applications, not one demonstrated covariant construction.
sections.title: Inputs → construction → claimed outputs

sections.text:
The simplest interpretation is that the same boundary energy is described using either surface gravity or its inverse length. Increasing area at fixed acceleration length increases \(U\); increasing acceleration length at fixed area decreases it. Calling the negative length derivative a generalized force makes the second change look like mechanical work. This is a work-coordinate interpretation, not evidence of a force acting on matter.

The thermal formulation makes the relationship especially transparent. Since \(T\propto L^{-1}\) and \(S\propto A\),
\[
dU=T\,dS+S\,dT,\qquad S\,dT=-F_L\,dL.
\]
The proposed length-work term therefore represents the temperature-variation part of the adopted heat-content potential. Thermal assumptions are unnecessary to calculate the derivative-defined force, but they reveal its relation to the familiar thermal split.

The two pressures must remain distinct. \(\Pi\) has units of energy per area, or force per length: it is an area-conjugate surface stress. \(P_L\) has units of energy per volume because an additional length divides that surface stress. The product \(AL\) is not generally the areal volume.

For Schwarzschild, differentiation must precede imposing \(A=4\pi R^2\) and \(L=2R\). Along that family, \(dL=2dR\), so
\[
F_R=2F_L=M\kappa,\qquad P_R=2P_L,\qquad U=3P_RV.
\]
Here \(M_U=M/2\); confusing these masses would obscure the factor of two. The proposed sum \(Mc^2=TS+F_LL\) contains two products each equal to \(U\). It is consequently an algebraic rewriting of \(Mc^2=2U=2TS\), not yet a physically independent partition into two energy reservoirs. It does not add a work term to the retained mass first law \(d(Mc^2)=T\,dS\).

For the FRW screen, \(L=R_A\) instead gives \(P=P_L\). With spherical area and the stipulated energy, \(E=3PV\), hence \(\rho=3P\). Substituting this relation into the usual energy-density formulation produces the printed screen-pressure equations. The screen pressure is not the bulk pressure \(p_m\), so \(P=\rho/3\) does not impose a radiation equation of state on cosmic matter. The manuscript supplies a change of variables and an equilibrium-screen identity, not an independent mechanism determining expansion or acceleration.
sections.title: Scientific review: What the construction means

sections.text:
The closest demonstrated antecedent is Parattu et al., arXiv:1303.1535. Its selected passages identify a horizon surface Hamiltonian with \(TS\), split its variation into \(T\delta S\) and \(S\delta T\), and relate those pieces to specified gravitational variables and their conjugate momenta. The manuscript therefore does not originate either this potential's thermal meaning or the existence of its two variation terms. Its length response reexpresses the second term through \(T\propto1/L\).

Hopfmüller–Freidel, arXiv:1611.03096, supplies selected derivations of null-boundary symplectic potentials, surface-gravity boundary actions, scalar canonical structure, and corner contributions. These establish a relevant canonical foundation while also showing that total variations and polarization choices matter. Odak et al., arXiv:2309.03854, explicitly displays several polarizations with different scalar \(\delta k\), expansion, and area-variation terms. Its selected discussion shows why boundary conditions and normal variations cannot be omitted when identifying a canonical response.

The selected membrane paper arXiv:1111.1242 already relates Einstein membrane surface pressure to horizon heat content through \(p_sA=TS\). Where clock, redshift, sign, and unit conventions agree, this is the manuscript's \(\Pi A=U\), not its three-dimensional \(P_L\). The distinction \(P_L=\Pi/L\) is essential to avoid presenting established membrane surface pressure as a newly discovered quantity.

Cai–Kim, hep-th/0501055, already connects apparent-horizon thermodynamics with Friedmann equations for nonzero as well as zero spatial curvature. Its displayed discussion qualifies the inverse-radius temperature assignment for a dynamical horizon. Akbar–Cai, hep-th/0609128, establishes a different, dynamical apparent-horizon formulation involving \(dE=T\,dS+W\,dV\), with \(W=(\rho-p_m)/2\) under its conventions, and distinguishes changing enclosed energy from heat flux across a temporarily fixed horizon. These are foundational precedents, but neither formula should be silently identified with the manuscript's positive-temperature equilibrium-screen relation \(dE=T\,dS-P\,dV\).
sections.title: Scientific review: Established foundations and overlap

sections.text:
The precisely identifiable proposal is to privilege \(L=c^2/\kappa\), motivated by its Rindler distance interpretation, as a work coordinate for an already adopted boundary potential; name its conjugate response \(F_L\); and distinguish normal-scale force density from area-conjugate surface stress and radius-conjugate pressure. A further proposed bridge identifies that derivative-defined coefficient in a selected action response.

Relative to Parattu et al., the possible distinction is the explicit mechanical interpretation and geometric normalization of the inverse-temperature coordinate, not the \(TS\) potential or its variation. Relative to the membrane result, it is the conversion from \(\Pi\) to \(\Pi/L\), together with careful work-coordinate transformations. Relative to the null-canonical papers, it would be an application and interpretation of an existing scalar response rather than a new canonical degree of freedom. The supplied passages do not settle whether these exact identifications were previously made elsewhere.

The canonical bridge could provide more than a convenient derivative notation if the author reconstructs the precise action, polarization, corner terms, admissible variations, and normalization that produce the stated response. The displayed Odak alternatives contain different coefficients of \(\delta k\) and, in some choices, accompanying area variations. Their reduction must therefore be demonstrated rather than inferred from the generic existence of surface-gravity conjugacy. This is an unresolved derivational requirement, not a demonstrated contradiction.

The cosmological proposal is narrower: screen-pressure variables organize established Einstein–FRW equations. Cai–Kim and Akbar–Cai substantially precede the horizon-thermodynamic setting, while Wang's abstract describes an evolving cosmological membrane with pressure corrections. The manuscript's separate instantaneous-equilibrium assignment does not yet replace those dynamical constructions.

No new observationally discriminating prediction, measurement protocol for \(F_L\), or departure from Einstein gravity is supplied. On this evidence, the advance may be a useful conceptual organization, but its distinctness and physical explanatory gain remain conditional.
sections.title: Scientific review: Conditional novelty and conceptual advance

sections.text:
Established content. The supplied literature already explains how horizon area and surface gravity enter boundary actions, canonical responses, membrane stresses, and thermal identities. The mathematical report supports the manuscript's specified scalar translations within that framework; it does not establish the framework anew.

Potential contribution. The most useful insight is a separation of quantities that can otherwise be conflated: an area-conjugate surface stress, an acceleration-length force density, and a pressure obtained after choosing a spherical-radius or volume coordinate. The Schwarzschild factor of two versus the FRW unit conversion makes this distinction concrete. If presented with a reproducible boundary prescription, the work could improve interpretation and bookkeeping across mechanical and thermal descriptions of horizon boundaries.

What would change. The proposed interpretation would organize the existing temperature-variation response as work in an acceleration-length coordinate. It would not, as presently developed, change the field equations, establish a new interaction, explain the microscopic origin of horizon entropy, or supply a new cause of cosmological acceleration. The FRW equations retain dependence on total bulk pressure and imported Einstein dynamics.

Evaluation. This is a plausible modest conceptual or pedagogical contribution, rather than demonstrated new physical content. Its value depends on whether the chosen length is physically privileged beyond its Rindler realization and whether the canonical identification survives the explicitly chosen boundary conventions. Claims of a unique physical force or independently meaningful energy partition would go beyond the available evidence. Extensions to unrestricted evolving boundaries remain prospective, and no new empirical test is provided. The present evidence permits neither an exhaustive novelty verdict nor a conclusion that the proposed interpretation is empirically established.
sections.title: Scientific review: Potential contribution to the field's explanation

sections.text:
Mathematical report. An actual report is supplied for package digest 218eb4ef06287c6920a1962a4c70f6133c27e188477b32dc47c18f3d62b0d2ef, using formal-lab-sympy-v2 and SymPy 1.14.0. All supplied claim entries have status checked, zero residual, and consistent dimensions under their declared definitions and domains; no contradicted or inconclusive entries appear. Examples include b1-g01_mass_acceleration_identity and b1-g01_pressure_surface_gravity for the main mechanical formulas; b2-g02_thermal_product for \(U=TS\); b3-schw_pressure_factor and b3-schw_mass_first_law for Schwarzschild; b4-frw_density_pressure and b4-frw_first_law_radius for the screen family; and b5-g05_canonical_force_coeff for the scalar coordinate transformation. These statuses concern the encoded scalar claims only. In particular, b3-potential_length_substitution is explicitly classified as a definition-restatement, not independent physical validation.

The cosmological checks must not be overstated. b4-frw_flat_pressure_rewrite uses the adopted apparent-radius relation; b4-frw_acceleration_coefficient_rewrite and b4-frw_conservation_expression_rewrite check substitutions and chain-rule expressions, not the truth or derivation of the acceleration and conservation laws. The curved-radius check represents a squared relation under a rational parametrization, not an independent proof of the original square-root assignment or unrestricted branch coverage.

Canonical and physical gaps. The supplied manuscript does not spell out the mixed boundary prescription, complete corner treatment, units and orientation restoration, or reduction from the cited null potential to its integrated scalar response. A scalar \(A\delta\kappa\) response is not the complete differential of \(U\) when area also varies. Fixed clock normalization is indispensable; Rindler fixes a useful observer-dependent geometric interpretation but does not establish a clock-independent force or a general proper-distance interpretation of \(L\). No local stress-tensor or operational traction derivation establishes \(P_L\) as a measured normal pressure. The null-boundary literature also requires attention to shear, normal variations, and admissible phase spaces; merely imposing zero expansion does not resolve every such issue.

The evolving FRW assignment needs a stated validity criterion and comparison with dynamical surface gravity, energy flux, and work density. Its equilibrium-radius identity alone supplies no evolution equation. No matter model, quantitative nonequilibrium correction, or observational discrimination is given.

Source and chronology limits. Only this supplied page is reviewed; the companion manuscripts mentioned at its end are unavailable. Primary evidence consists of selected passages, not complete readings; other papers support only their labelled abstract-level comparisons. Absence from selected passages is not absence from an entire paper, and bounded searches cannot establish priority. The 2022 multi-author INSPIRE record and the similarly titled 2023 thesis record have overlapping thesis-like descriptions, warranting bibliographic clarification.

The assessment reference is 2026-10-25T21:15:41.111Z. The manuscript's explicit date, 22 October 2026, precedes it and is not future-dated. No supplied explicit date establishes a future-dated literature record; year-only metadata leaves finer priority unresolved. ArXiv years must not be confused with later journal years: Harlow–Wu is recorded as a 2019 preprint with a 2020 journal DOI record, while arXiv:1111.1242 is a 2011 preprint with a 2012 journal DOI record. This review does not approve a revision, modify the equation-check report, or authorize publication of its conclusions.

sections.title: Assessment basis and current evidence

sections.text: With the prescribed potential and fixed constants, \(U=c^4A/(8\pi GL)\). Independent derivatives give \(\Pi=c^4/(8\pi GL)\) and \(F_L=Ac^4/(8\pi GL^2)\), hence \(F_L=U/L=M_U\kappa\) and \(P_L=\kappa^2/(8\pi G)\). These formulas and the printed complete differential are supported by the supplied exact checks. The minus sign belongs to the length contribution in \(dU\); positive work is a separately identified quantity. For an invertible smooth change \(L=L(q)\), the work coefficient transforms as \(F_q=F_L\,dL/dq\), preserving the work one-form. Thermal inputs then give \(U=TS\), \(\Pi\,dA=T\,dS\), and the corresponding scale leg \(S\,dT=-F_L\,dL\). The mechanical definitions themselves contain no temperature or entropy input. None of these identities alone asserts a material force law.
sections.title: Mechanical construction and thermal translation

sections.text: The supplied calculation starts from Minkowski coordinates with \(X^0=(\rho+c^2/a)\sinh(a\tau/c)\) and \(X^1=(\rho+c^2/a)\cosh(a\tau/c)\). The pullback gives \(ds^2=-c^2(1+a\rho/c^2)^2d\tau^2+d\rho^2+dy^2+dz^2\). The reference observer at \(\rho=0\) has proper time \(\tau\) and proper acceleration \(a\). Constant-\(\tau\) slices are orthogonal to that observer, and their normal distance to the wedge-boundary endpoint is \(\int_{-c^2/a}^{0}d\rho=c^2/a\). The transverse area is independent of this normal scale. Thus the concrete statement at line 38 is supported, rather than merely assumed algebraically. The result fixes the normalization for this observer and slice; it says nothing universal about curved-horizon proper distance or canonical actions.
sections.title: Rindler normalization is geometrically established in the stated domain

sections.text: After taking the independent-coordinate derivative, restriction to \(A=4\pi R^2\) and \(L=2R\) yields \(F_L=c^4/(8G)\), \(F_R=2F_L=M\kappa\), and \(P_R=2P_L\). These are consistent transformed work coefficients, not competing universal pressure definitions. Along the family, \(dU/dR=c^4/(4G)\), whereas \(T\,dS/dR=c^4/(2G)\); the difference is exactly the retained work leg. The source correctly retains \(d(Mc^2)=T\,dS\). Its equal-product sum is supported algebraically, while the companion Horizon Boundary Mechanics: Force, Pressure, and Work from the Einstein Boundary Potential, Section 4, page 4, and Section 5.2, page 5, explicitly rules out interpreting the products as independent stores or adding the scale leg again to the mass law.
sections.title: Schwarzschild work factors and the mass law

sections.text:
The retrieved Hopfmüller–Freidel passages, especially Section IV Equations (60), (63) and (71) and Section V's scalar momentum discussion, support a rate/area scalar structure and the role of retained exact variations. Odak and collaborators, Section 3 Equation (3.34), display distinct polarizations; their Section 4.2 and Appendix B explain why polarization and boundary-data choices matter. These alternatives cannot be equated indiscriminately.

The supplied companion Horizon Boundary Mechanics: Force, Pressure, and Work from the Einstein Boundary Potential, Section 3, page 2, Equations (10)–(12), makes an explicit selection: \(\mu=\hat\kappa+\theta/2\), an area-polarized scalar term, and addition of an exact boundary variation to obtain an area-weighted \(\delta\mu\) response. Page 3, Equations (13)–(15), imposes both \(\theta=0\) and \(\delta\theta=0\), uses \(\kappa=c^2\hat\kappa\), and restores the physical time measure. Converting a length parameter by \(dv=c\,d\tau\) with the Einstein action normalization gives the displayed \(c^2/(8\pi G)\) coefficient. Uniform stationary reduction gives the one-page response; local length response gives pressure, and its area integral gives force.

Crucially, page 3 distinguishes a derivative across nearby boundary-value problems from variations fixing the source within one conservative problem. Thus the primary-source observation that fixing the mixed source can force its variation to vanish is not a contradiction of the companion's response derivative. Other canonical sectors are controlled or excluded by the scalar selection, not claimed to vanish merely because expansion vanishes. Section 3.1, pages 3–4, Equations (18)–(21), further checks the stationary coefficient through \(J_\eta=Ac^3/(8\pi G)\), boost rate \(\kappa/c\), and fixed-duration boost variation.

The supplied static-horizon-momentum-variation computation independently supports the static density coefficient with its stated outward orientation. The scalar pullback then has the checked negative sign because \(d\kappa/dL=-c^2/L^2\). These strands support the selected argument. They do not certify an arbitrary null-boundary variational principle or all normal, shear, spin-1 and corner variations. No specific remaining mismatch with lines 72–78 is demonstrated by the supplied evidence.
sections.title: A real restricted canonical derivation, not an unrestricted certification

sections.text:
The source declares instantaneous equilibrium at line 54 and separates evolving FRW from stationary worldtubes at lines 79–80. With \(L=R_A\), the accepted Einstein spherical inputs give \(E=c^4R_A/(2G)\), \(P_{\rm screen}=c^4/(8\pi GR_A^2)=\rho/3\), and \(T_{\rm CK}=\hbar c/(2\pi k_B R_A)\). Directly, \(dE/dR_A=c^4/(2G)\), \(T_{\rm CK}dS/dR_A=c^4/G\), and \(P_{\rm screen}dV/dR_A=c^4/(2G)\). Thus the printed screen-state differential is exactly consistent under these assignments.

Cai–Kim Section 2, particularly the discussion at S2.p4.2 and the summary at S5.p1.1, uses a momentarily fixed-horizon matter-flux construction and explains the approximate thermodynamic interpretation for an evolving horizon. Akbar–Cai Sections 3 and 6 instead distinguish changing enclosed energy from that flux and use the dynamical unified law with \(W=(\rho-p_m)/2\). The dynamical Hayward rate contains the factor \(1-\dot R_A/(2HR_A)\), conventionally in \(\kappa_H=-c^2R_A^{-1}[1-\dot R_A/(2HR_A)]\); it is not the positive Cai–Kim rate used here. Accordingly, the oriented dynamical relation \(dE=T_{\rm dyn}dS+W\,dV\) is not the same allocation as the manuscript's screen identity.

Companion Section 5.3, pages 5–6, explicitly develops this distinction. Neither the primary passages nor the numbered manuscript require identifying screen pressure with bulk pressure or transferring the stationary canonical restrictions to FRW. The formulas at lines 60–70 are correct rewrites of accepted Einstein–FRW dynamics using \(\rho=3P\). They introduce no new dynamics and establish no exact equilibrium thermal state throughout arbitrary evolution.

sections.text: Parattu and collaborators' Section 5.2, Equations (111)–(113), and Section 6 already supply the relevant horizon heat-content and thermal/canonical split in their stated static or local-Rindler regimes and variables. Hopfmüller–Freidel and Odak and collaborators already establish the null scalar structure and polarization dependence. The manuscript's defensible distinction is therefore the explicit length-conjugate interpretation, its geometric normalization and its coordinated treatment of length, radius and areal-volume work. This can improve understanding without a new observation or interaction. Its strongest explanatory payoff is removal of apparent sign and factor discrepancies between representations. The bounded search does not determine whether that exact presentation is historically first, and metadata-only records cannot settle the question.

Its printed date, 22 October 2026, precedes the supplied assessment reference date. sections.title: Assessment target and current evidence

sections.text: For independent positive \(A,L\), the adopted potential is \(U=c^4A/(8\pi GL)\). The supplied exact checks establish \(\Pi=c^4/(8\pi GL)=U/A\), \(F_L=Ac^4/(8\pi GL^2)=U/L=M_U\kappa\), and \(P_L=F_L/A=\Pi/L=\kappa^2/(8\pi G)\). Both coefficients of \(dU=\Pi\,dA-F_L\,dL\) and of \(A\,d\Pi=-F_L\,dL\) are checked. These identities require no temperature or entropy input, as p1-l080 states. They establish the derivative-defined responses, but the choice of gravitational potential and the selected action's physical conjugacy are separate questions. The later canonical evidence addresses that second question in a restricted domain. Neither \(F_L=M_U\kappa\) nor the name pressure asserts a new force acting on matter. Also, \(AL\) is not silently identified with spherical areal volume.
sections.title: The mechanical chain is correct under the prescribed potential

sections.text: The supplied coordinate pullback gives \(ds^2=-c^2(1+a\rho/c^2)^2d\tau^2+d\rho^2+dy^2+dz^2\), with the reference observer at \(\rho=0\). Its computed proper acceleration is \(a\), and constant-\(\tau\) slices are orthogonal to its four-velocity. The wedge boundary is at the normal-coordinate limit \(\rho=-c^2/a\), so the proper rest-slice distance is \(\int_{-c^2/a}^{0}d\rho=c^2/a\). The transverse metric gives patch area independent of that normal coordinate and acceleration. Thus p1-l038's specific geometric assertion is supported by actual metric, connection and distance calculations. This calibrates the normalization for that observer and slice; it is not a proof that inverse surface gravity is a universal curved-horizon proper distance, or that the wedge boundary is a material surface experiencing a force.
sections.title: Rindler supplies the claimed geometric calibration

sections.text:
The supporting source is Horizon Boundary Mechanics: Force, Pressure, and Work from the Einstein Boundary Potential (seven-page companion), Section 3, pages 2–3, at https://jttyler.com/papers/horizon-pressure-paper.pdf#page=2 and #page=3. It supplies \(\mu=\widehat\kappa+\theta/2\) and the exchange from area to rate polarization. Hopfmüller–Freidel's equation (71) and scalar-momentum discussion support this structure; Odak et al.'s equation (3.34) demonstrates why distinct polarizations must not be interchanged indiscriminately.

The restricted kernel goes beyond that citation comparison. In a fixed Gaussian-null chart it constructs all 64 connection variations from a general cut metric and first metric/variation jets, then computes the EH boundary current at \(r=0\). With its stated orientation, it checks the decomposition into \(-\mu\,\delta\epsilon_S\), a retained shear pairing and an exact variation of \(\epsilon_S(\widehat\kappa+\theta)\), with the Einstein normalization. It explicitly varies \(I_{\rm rate}=I_{\rm EH}-B_0+B_\mu\), obtaining the scalar rate form \(\epsilon_S\delta\mu/(8\pi G)\) while retaining shear response. Selection of those boundary functionals remains a physical prescription; the local reduction itself is computed, not merely cited.
sections.title: The local Einstein–Hilbert canonical bridge is now computed

sections.text:
The page explicitly imposes both \(\theta=0\) and \(\delta\theta=0\). The kernel checks their reduction of the scalar source to \(\widehat\kappa\), and tracks the exact action shift \(-(A_f-A_i)/(16\pi G)\) in geometric units. Tangent nonexpansion throughout the fixed interval gives \(\delta A_f=\delta A_i\), not necessarily zero variation at either endpoint. Other corner and canonical responses remain controlled premises, not consequences of fixed cut locations alone.

The checked Jacobians \(dv=c\,d\tau\) and \(\widehat\kappa=\kappa/c^2\) restore \(\Theta^{(0)}=\int d\tau\,Ac^2\delta\kappa/(8\pi G)\) for the uniform stationary mode. The checked pullback \(\delta\kappa=-c^2\delta L/L^2\) then gives equation (9). The explicit reduced generating-functional variation and fixed-duration derivative yield \(-\Delta\tau F_L\) for a constant source variation. Companion Section 3.1, pages 3–4, supplies the consistent stationary area–boost route; the separate static metric check independently supports the static-sector coefficient.

Expected-nonzero controls show why nonexpansion alone cannot remove shear, why the selected one-form is not \(\delta U\), and why a source-dependent exact counterterm can change the one-form while preserving its two-form. These are counterexamples to stronger inferences, not contradictions of this prescription-dependent manuscript. No concrete remaining sign or normalization inconsistency is identified.
sections.title: Variation restrictions, endpoints and physical normalization

sections.text:
Accepting the stated temperature and entropy laws, the checked identities give \(U=TS\) and \(\Pi\,dA=T\,dS\). Consequently the length leg corresponds to \(S\,dT=-F_L\,dL\). Parattu et al., Section 5.2.1, equations (111)–(113), and the supplied conclusion passages establish substantial prior thermal-canonical content in their specified static/local-Rindler regimes.

For Schwarzschild, the independent-area derivative is taken before imposing \(A=4\pi R^2\) and \(L=2R\). The checked work transformation gives \(F_R=2F_L=M\kappa\), \(P_R=2P_L\), and \(U=3P_RV\). Here \(M_U=M/2\). The checked sum \(Mc^2=TS+F_LL\) has two products each equal to \(U\); it is not a unique division into stored energies. The companion, Sections 4 and 5.2, pages 4–5, makes that interpretation explicit. The separate checked mass first law remains \(d(Mc^2)=T\,dS\); appending the scale leg to it would double-count the family variation, but the page does not do so.
sections.title: Thermal translation and Schwarzschild do not add a second energy reservoir

sections.text:
The page assigns \(L=R_A\) in a separate instantaneous-equilibrium screen sector. With spherical area, areal volume and Einstein Misner–Sharp energy, the checked results are \(U=E=c^4R_A/(2G)\), \(P=P_L=\rho/3\), and \(dE=T_{\rm CK}dS-P\,dV\). Explicitly, the radius coefficients are \(dE/dR_A=c^4/(2G)\), \(T_{\rm CK}dS/dR_A=c^4/G\), and \(P\,dV/dR_A=c^4/(2G)\), so the sign and factor balance is correct.

Cai–Kim, Section 2, discusses the inverse-radius temperature and its dynamical qualification. Akbar–Cai, Section 3 and the comparison in Section 6, distinguishes enclosed-energy change from horizon-crossing heat and uses a dynamical law with \(W=(\rho-p_m)/2\). Its Hayward rate contains the evolution factor \(1-\dot R_A/(2HR_A)\), unlike the declared positive CK calibration. Therefore \(dE=T_{\rm dyn}dS+W\,dV\) must not be identified term by term with the manuscript's screen-state identity. The companion, Section 5.3, pages 5–6, explicitly distinguishes them. Neither the page nor that context equates \(P\) with bulk matter pressure. No incompatible-convention claim is found.
sections.title: The FRW screen identity is coherent and convention-specific

sections.text: With total energy density \(\rho=3P\), the established Einstein expansion equation becomes \(H^2+kc^2/a^2=(8\pi G/c^2)P\). The standard acceleration and conservation equations similarly become the printed expressions involving \(P+p_m\) and \(\dot P+H(3P+p_m)\). The supplied scalar checks verify the substitutions, including the differentiated density relation; they do not independently establish the field equations or force a conservation expression to vanish. Accepting those familiar Einstein inputs is appropriate because p1-l069–p1-l070 expressly presents a representation of the same equations. Consistent total vacuum contributions can be included in that standard accounting. The stationary canonical restriction must not be transferred onto this explicitly separate screen assignment. Exact screen-state identities do not establish exact equilibrium radiation or thermality during arbitrary FRW evolution, but the page makes no such unrestricted claim.
sections.title: The cosmological equations are valid rewrites, not a new derivation of gravity

sections.text:
The closest demonstrated antecedents are the TS surface Hamiltonian and thermal split in 1303.1535, the scalar null-boundary structures in 1611.03096 and 2309.03854, and the membrane surface-pressure relation in 1111.1242. The last concerns an area-conjugate surface quantity, matching \(\Pi\) under matched conventions, not automatically the three-dimensional force density \(P_L\). The explicit use of acceleration length as a calibrated work coordinate is therefore a supported operational distinction, although it may be a modest conceptual advance rather than new dynamics.

The discovered papers 1111.1242 and 2008.10551 are review-discovered context, not entries secretly attributed to the author's bibliography. In particular, the fixed-surface-gravity boundary structure in the selected 2008.10551 construction does not contradict a different prescription that permits source variation across boundary-value problems. Abstract-only records and irrelevant keyword hits do not establish mathematical equivalence or contrary prior art. The bounded arXiv, Crossref and INSPIRE search cannot certify priority. The unavailable full manuscript is not assumed, and the supplied companion is used only at its actual cited locators.

claimSourceJudgments.reason: Within the specified potential and area-response convention, the checked area coefficient supplies the area-work term. The retrieved membrane and thermal passages substantively support its surface-stress interpretation when conventions are matched. This does not assert a universal material stress tensor or a unique action prescription.

The independent-coordinate derivative and the restricted action-source pullback support force paired with acceleration-length change. The companion's selected prescription supplies the physical source-response context; the result is not inferred from dimensional resemblance to mass times acceleration alone.

Read as a smooth locally invertible scalar work-coordinate change, this is the covector transformation rule: the new coefficient includes the coordinate Jacobian. The Schwarzschild and surface-gravity-to-length checks provide actual instances. It is not an assertion of invariance under arbitrary changes of action, polarization or gauge.

On the adopted Schwarzschild family, L=2R gives equal fractional size changes, while the transformed coefficient preserves the work. The statement describes the same family variation; it need not mean displacement of a second physical surface situated at twice the horizon radius.

Accepting established Einstein–FRW dynamics, the checked relation rho=3P, acceleration-coefficient substitution, differentiated conservation substitution and curved-radius rewrite support precisely a screen-pressure representation of those equations. This does not promote the substitutions into an independent derivation of Einstein dynamics.

The sum and equal products are checked. Calling their organization a mass-energy decomposition is a reasonable interpretation when, as the companion explicitly explains, the terms are products associated with different response directions of one potential, not independently stored energies or a unique physical partition.
